title: Missing type for PEP695 `TypeAliasType` vs `TypeAlias` when using `TypeAdapter`

judge.reasoning: The issue asks that `TypeAdapter(my_type)` on a `type` statement alias yield the aliased type, as it does for a `TypeAlias`. Patch A fixes this at the root by typing `TypeAdapter.__init__` (and related APIs like `validate_as`, `ValidateAs`, `create_model`, serializer `return_type`) with PEP 747 `TypeForm[T]`. Under PEP 747 a `TypeAliasType` instance evaluates to `TypeForm[<aliased type>]`, so `T` is inferred as `list[dict[str, list[int]]]` and `reveal_type(res)` matches the `TypeAlias` case. The accompanying typechecking tests (`type_adapter.py`, new `type_form.py`, `pipeline_api.py`) assert precise inference for `Annotated`, `Union`, and `|` forms and drop the old `assert-type` ignores, which would fail before the change. Patch B only adds an overload that catches `TypeAliasType` instances and returns `TypeAdapter[Any]`; its own comments admit the real type cannot be extracted without PEP 747. That silences the red squiggle but leaves `res` as `Any`, so the issue's actual expectation (correct type shown) is not met, and its tests only check assignability to `list[int]` (which `Any` trivially satisfies) rather than `assert_type` of the precise result. Patch A does carry unrelated churn (pyrefly ignore comments across many test files, a CI pyright version pin, a Makefile tweak) and some edge changes like `_FromFieldInfoInputs.annotation` losing `| None`, which add review risk, but these do not undermine the fix. B is the safer, smaller change, but it masks the symptom rather than resolving the reported behaviour, so A is the better fix on correctness and tests.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

There seems to be a difference between the type that is returned from TypeAdapter when used on a PEP695 `TypeAliasType` compared to when it is used on a `TypeAlias`. See example below. When `TypeAdapter` is used on a `TypeAlias`, the correct type is shown. However, when the `TypeAliasType` is used, the type is shown as `TypeAliasType`. This causes the type-checker to see red. 

### Example Code

```Python
from typing import TypeAlias, reveal_type

from pydantic import TypeAdapter

my_type_alias: TypeAlias = list[dict[str, list[int]]]
x: my_type_alias = [{"a": [1, 2, 3]}]

res = TypeAdapter(type=my_type_alias).validate_python(x)
reveal_type(res)  # type of res is "list[dict[str, list[int]]]"


type my_type = list[dict[str, list[int]]]
x: my_type = [{"a": [1, 2, 3]}]

res = TypeAdapter(type=my_type).validate_python(x)
reveal_type(res)  # type of res is "TypeAliasType"
```


### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```Text
pydantic version: 2.6.3
        pydantic-core version: 2.16.3
          pydantic-core build: profile=release pgo=true
                 install path: /usr/local/lib/python3.12/site-packages/pydantic
               python version: 3.12.2 (main, Feb 13 2024, 09:17:46) [GCC 12.2.0]
                     platform: Linux-5.15.133.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2-x86_64-with-glibc2.36
             related packages: pyright-1.1.352 pyright-1.1.353 typing_extensions-4.10.0 pydantic-extra-types-2.6.0 fastapi-0.110.0 pydantic-settings-2.2.1
                       commit: unknown
```

title: Mypy internal error when subclassing a generic model with a recursive type variable

judge.reasoning:
The production change is functionally identical in both patches: import `has_placeholder`, and in `transform()` return False (deferring unless on the final iteration) when any collected field type still contains a placeholder. Both also guard against infinite deferral with `final_iteration`. Patch B's split of the `None` check and placeholder check is marginally clearer but not materially different. The independent tests confirm both fix the crash and preserve correct field typing.

The difference is in tests. Patch B adds a dedicated module `generics_recursive.py`, registers it in `test_mypy.py`, and supplies the corresponding expected-output file under `outputs/mypy-plugin_ini/`, which is how pydantic's mypy test harness works. It covers the exact issue scenario, a forward reference to a later-defined subclass, and negative cases that verify mypy still reports real list-item type errors rather than silently accepting anything. Patch A only appends to the existing `generics.py` module without updating its corresponding expected-output file; since the harness compares module source against the stored output, that existing case would likely fail or be out of sync. Patch A's test also includes a stray `"""<link>"""` docstring that is noise, and it lacks any negative assertion. B's tests are complete, correctly wired, and more rigorous, so B is the better patch.

title: Cannot use model_dump(include=...) with @model_serializer (raises PydanticOmit)

judge.reasoning:
The issue's ask is that `model_dump(include=...)` work when a wrap `@model_serializer` calls `handler(self, info)`, a call shape the base repo's own `WrapSerializer` docstring demonstrates. Patch B addresses this directly: in `SerializationCallable.__call__` it drops an `index_key` that is a `SerializationInfo` instance before applying include/exclude filtering, so the issue's exact example returns `{'bar': 123}`, and exclude/JSON variants also work. The independent tests confirm this (all four pass on B, all fail on base). B also corrects the docstring to `handler(value)` and adds tests at both the pydantic-core level (typed_dict with wrap serializer, include/exclude/json) and the pydantic level (model_serializer and field_serializer), all of which fail on base and pass with the fix.

Patch A takes the position that passing `info` to the handler is user error: it keeps the `PydanticOmit` path replaced by a `TypeError` for non-int/non-str index keys and rewrites the docstring example to stop passing `info`. title: Some Field attributes lost in JSON schema when using RootModel

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the three reported gaps (examples, deprecated, title) and pass every independent test. The difference is at the edges. Patch A reads `cls.__pydantic_fields__['root'].title` without distinguishing an explicitly set title from one injected by `field_title_generator` (pydantic writes generated titles back onto FieldInfo during core schema generation), so a RootModel configured with a field title generator would get e.g. 'ROOT' as its model title. Patch B guards this via `_attributes_set` and adds a test for it. Patch B also folds the root field's `deprecated` into the existing `__deprecated__` branch (handling the message-string and empty-string forms) rather than adding a separate block, and reuses the `__pydantic_root_model__` check already used later in the same function, removing the ad-hoc RootModel import. Its title precedence (config title > root field title > model_title_generator) is explicit and tested, whereas Patch A's ordering makes model_title_generator silently beat an explicit Field(title=...). Tests: B covers nested $defs usage, deprecated-as-message, title generator interactions, and config override; A's tests are reasonable but narrower. Scope and churn are comparable; B's small refactor is low-risk and clarifies the fix. B is the better fix.

title: mypy `[arg-type]`-error when passing in type that can be converted to `RootModel`

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause identically: they register the `_RootModelMetaclass` in the metaclass hook and stop `add_initializer` from bailing out on `RootModel` itself because it has a hand-written `__init__`, so the plugin-generated `__init__` (typed `Any` when `init_typed` is unset) replaces the stub signature and `RootModel[float]('1.0')` no longer errors under the plugin. Under the default (no-plugin) config both patches leave the error in place, which is the only sensible outcome there. On correctness for the reported issue they are equivalent.

Patch A goes further: it changes the `root` argument kind from unconditional `ARG_OPT` to `ARG_POS` unless a default exists (keeping it optional only on `RootModel` itself via a new `force_optional` condition). This is a behavior change outside the issue's ask: existing user code like `Pets1()` that previously type-checked now gets a new `call-arg` error (visible in A's updated expected outputs). It may well be the more accurate runtime model, but it is an unrelated tightening bundled into a bug fix, adding regression risk for downstream users and obscuring the minimal fix. It also adds a new `mypy-plugin-strict.ini` test case whose outputs mostly re-verify unchanged behavior.

Patch A's tests are somewhat broader (keyword `root=` form, strict config), which is a point in its favor. Patch B's tests cover the issue's exact scenario plus the subclass case across the plugin and non-plugin configs, which is adequate and would fail before the change under the plugin config.

Patch B's edit is narrower, uses an equally valid `self._cls.fullname` check, and leaves the established `ARG_OPT` semantics for `root` untouched. Given equal correctness, B wins on scope and risk; A's extra test coverage does not outweigh the unrequested semantic change.

title: Decimal JSON schema pattern uses lookahead regex unsupported by pydantic-core

judge.reasoning: Both patches make the emitted Decimal pattern compilable by pydantic-core, and the independent tests pass on both. Patch A fixes the root cause directly: it rewrites the four constraint cases without look-around, keeps the same anchored structure (`^[+-]?(?:...)$`), handles the decimal_places > max_digits edge via `min(decimal_places, max_digits)`, enumerates integer-width alternatives for the max_digits-only case, and preserves existing behaviour (leading/trailing zeros, rejection of '', '.', '+-'). Its new tests compile each pattern through `TypeAdapter(Annotated[str, StringConstraints(pattern=...)])` and check both valid and invalid strings for every constraint combination, plus a direct reproduction of the issue's model_json_schema round-trip. These would fail on base with SchemaError and pass after. Patch B resolves the issue mainly by removing the pattern from the default JSON schema entirely and moving pattern generation behind an opt-in `get_decimal_pattern` hook. That is a user-visible feature removal (max_digits/decimal_places no longer reflected in the schema by default, docs changed to 'N/A') that the issue did not ask for, and it means ordinary users still get no pydantic-core-compatible pattern unless they subclass the generator. Alongside that it adds a large redesign: separate validation/serialization patterns modelling `str(Decimal)` output including scientific notation thresholds, an `_int_range_pattern` helper, allow_inf_nan handling, and unrelated code movement of `_HashableJsonValue`. The extra machinery is extensively tested, but it is well beyond scope and the serialization-pattern logic (exponent ranges, E-7 cutoff, per-k enumeration) is intricate and high-risk relative to the ask. Existing pattern tests in B were rewritten to pass through a custom generator, so they no longer exercise default behaviour. Patch A is the focused, correct, well-tested fix; Patch B fixes the symptom by dropping the feature and bundles a risky redesign.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

  Pydantic v2 emits a JSON schema for Decimal fields that includes a regex pattern with a negative lookahead `((?!...))`. This pattern cannot be compiled by `pydantic-core`'s Rust regex crate, which does not support look-around assertions.

  This means the JSON schema pydantic produces for Decimal cannot be round-tripped back through pydantic's own validation  e.g. constructing a `TypeAdapter` with `StringConstraints(pattern=...)` using the emitted pattern fails with a `SchemaError`.

  This is a practical problem for any tooling that reconstructs pydantic types from emitted JSON schemas (e.g. MCP structured content parsing via FastMCP).


### Example Code

```Python
"""Minimal reproduction: Decimal JSON schema pattern uses lookahead unsupported by pydantic-core.

Pydantic generates a JSON schema for Decimal fields with a regex pattern that uses
a negative lookahead (?!...). When that schema is round-tripped back through pydantic
(e.g. via TypeAdapter with StringConstraints), pydantic-core's Rust regex engine
rejects it because it does not support look-around assertions.
"""

from decimal import Decimal
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import BaseModel, StringConstraints, TypeAdapter


class MyModel(BaseModel):
    amount: Decimal


def test_decimal_json_schema_pattern_roundtrips_through_pydantic_core():
    schema = MyModel.model_json_schema()

    # Decimal emits an anyOf with a string variant carrying the pattern
    string_variant = next(v for v in schema['properties']['amount']['anyOf'] if v.get('type') == 'string')
    pattern = string_variant['pattern']

    # The emitted pattern contains a negative lookahead:
    assert '(?!' in pattern

    # Feeding it back into StringConstraints fails with:
    #   SchemaError: regex parse error: look-around ... is not supported
    ConstrainedStr = Annotated[str, StringConstraints(pattern=pattern)]
    TypeAdapter(ConstrainedStr)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    test_decimal_json_schema_pattern_roundtrips_through_pydantic_core()
```

+# Decimal JSON Schema pattern utilities.
+# Note: while we could use `\d` to represent digits (`Decimal` objects allow Unicode decimal digits), we use [0-9] instead:
+# - to reduce complexity (`\d` expands to a large set, and with `max_digits`/`decimal_places` constraints set, it can blow
+#   the compile limit on some engines).
+# - [0-9] is a portable pattern (e.g. `\d` is equivalent to `[0-9]` in ECMA (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Regular_expressions/Character_class_escape#d)
+#   while it allows any Unicode decimal digit in Python.

+def _repeat(atom: str, min_count: int, max_count: int) -> str:
+    """Build a regex repetition of `atom` between `min_count` and `max_count` times (inclusive), using the shortest quantifier."""
+    if min_count > max_count or max_count == 0:
+        return ''
+    if min_count == max_count:
+        return atom if min_count == 1 else f'{atom}{{{min_count}}}'
+    if (min_count, max_count) == (0, 1):
+        return f'{atom}?'
+    return f'{atom}{{{min_count},{max_count}}}'
+
+
+def _int_range_pattern(max_value: int) -> str:
+    """Build a regex matching the integers between 1 and `max_value` (inclusive), without leading zeros."""
+    digits = str(max_value)
+    length = len(digits)
+    alts: list[str] = [f'[1-9]{_repeat("[0-9]", k - 1, k - 1)}' for k in range(1, length)]
+    for i, char in enumerate(digits):
+        d = int(char)
+        low = 1 if i == 0 else 0
+        high = d if i == length - 1 else d - 1
+        if high >= low:
+            char_class = str(low) if low == high else f'[{low}-{high}]'
+            alts.append(f'{digits[:i]}{char_class}{_repeat("[0-9]", length - i - 1, length - i - 1)}')
+    return alts[0] if len(alts) == 1 else f'(?:{"|".join(alts)})'

+def _decimal_validation_pattern(max_digits: int | None, decimal_places: int | None, allow_inf_nan: bool) -> str:

+    exponent = r'[eE][+-]?[0-9]+'  # e.g. e5, E5, e-7
+    # e.g. Infinity, inf, NaN, sNaN, NaN123 (case-insensitive). Spelled out explicitly, as inline flags
+    # aren't supported by all regular expression engines:
+    non_finite = r'|[iI][nN][fF](?:[iI][nN][iI][tT][yY])?|[sS]?[nN][aA][nN][0-9]*' if allow_inf_nan else ''
+    if max_digits is None and decimal_places is None:
+        return rf'^[+-]?(?:{number}(?:{exponent})?{non_finite})$'
+
+    alts: list[str] = []
+    if max_digits is not None and decimal_places is not None:

+        whole = max(0, max_digits - decimal_places)

+def _decimal_serialization_pattern(max_digits: int | None, decimal_places: int | None, allow_inf_nan: bool) -> str:
+    """Build the decimal pattern for the `'serialization'` mode.
+
+    Decimals are serialized using `str()`, producing either:
+
+    - The plain notation (`'123.45'`), when the exponent is lower than or equal to 0 and the adjusted
+      exponent is greater than or equal to -6.
+    - The scientific notation otherwise (`'1E+3'`, `'1.5E-7'`, `'0E-10'`), with a single digit before
+      the optional decimal point and an always signed exponent.
+
+    Trailing zeros of the decimal part are preserved by `str()`, but aren't counted by the validation logic.
+    """
+
+    def frac_part(places: int) -> str:
+        return rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, places)}0*' if places else r'\.0+'
+
+    alts: list[str] = []
+
+    # Plain notation:
+    if max_digits is not None and decimal_places is not None:
+        whole = max(0, max_digits - decimal_places)
+        places = min(max_digits, decimal_places)
+        int_part = f'(?:0|[1-9]{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, whole - 1)})' if whole else '0'
+        alts.append(f'{int_part}(?:{frac_part(places)})?')
+    elif max_digits is not None:
+        # The whole part and decimal part must have at most `max_digits` digits in total,
+        # so we enumerate the possible widths of the whole part:
+        alts.append(rf'0(?:\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, max_digits)}0*)?')
+        alts += [
+            f'[1-9]{_repeat("[0-9]", whole - 1, whole - 1)}(?:{frac_part(max_digits - whole)})?'
+            for whole in range(1, max_digits + 1)
+        ]
+    elif decimal_places is not None:
+        alts.append(f'(?:0|[1-9][0-9]*)(?:{frac_part(decimal_places)})?')
+    else:
+        alts.append(r'(?:0|[1-9][0-9]*)(?:\.[0-9]+)?')
+
+    # Zero with an exponent (e.g. `'0E-10'`), which normalizes to zero and thus satisfies any constraint:
+    alts.append(r'0E[+-][1-9][0-9]*')
+
+    # Scientific notation with a positive exponent `k` (e.g. `'1.5E+3'`): the value has `k + 1` whole digits
+    # and no decimal places:
+    if max_digits is None:
+        alts.append(r'[1-9](?:\.[0-9]+)?E\+[1-9][0-9]*')
+    else:
+        max_exponent = max_digits - (decimal_places or 0) - 1
+        if max_exponent >= 1:
+            alts.append(rf'[1-9](?:\.[0-9]+)?E\+{_int_range_pattern(max_exponent)}')
+
+    # Scientific notation with a negative exponent `k` (`k >= 7`, e.g. `'1.5E-7'`): the value has no whole digits,
+    # and `k` + (the number of significant decimal digits of the coefficient) decimal places:
+    if max_digits is None and decimal_places is None:
+        alts.append(r'[1-9](?:\.[0-9]+)?E-[1-9][0-9]*')
+    else:
+        max_places = min(c for c in (max_digits, decimal_places) if c is not None)
+        alts += [f'[1-9](?:{frac_part(max_places - k)})?E-{k}' for k in range(7, max_places + 1)]
+
+    if allow_inf_nan:
+        # `str()` produces `'Infinity'`, `'NaN'` and `'sNaN'` (with an optional payload):
+        alts += ['Infinity', 's?NaN[0-9]*']
+
+    return rf'^-?(?:{"|".join(alts)})$'
 
 
 def _deduplicate_schemas(schemas: Iterable[JsonDict]) -> list[JsonDict]:
     return list({_make_json_hashable(schema): schema for schema in schemas}.values())
 
 
+_HashableJsonValue: TypeAlias = (
+    int | float | str | bool | None | tuple['_HashableJsonValue', ...] | tuple[tuple[str, '_HashableJsonValue'], ...]
+)
+
+
 def _make_json_hashable(value: JsonValue) -> _HashableJsonValue:
     if isinstance(value, dict):
         return tuple(sorted((k, _make_json_hashable(v)) for k, v in value.items()))

title: Decimal JSON schema pattern rejects pydantic's own scientific notation serialization output (v2.12 regression)

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make pydantic's own `model_dump_json()` output for scientific-notation Decimals acceptable against the serialization schema, and all independent tests pass on both. They get there very differently.

Patch A does exactly what the issue proposes: it appends an exponent alternative (`|^[+-]?(?:\d+\.?\d*|\.\d+)[eE][+-]?\d+$`) to the existing pattern in `get_decimal_pattern`, keeps the `max_digits`/`decimal_places` pattern feature intact, documents in a comment that constraints are not enforced on the exponent branch (an acknowledged, bounded loosening), and updates the doc/test expectations. Its new tests are meaningful: they serialize real models with and without constraints, assert the output actually contains an `E`, and check both `re.search` and `re.fullmatch` against the generated pattern; separate accept/reject tables cover malformed exponent strings. These fail on base and pass with the fix.

Patch B resolves the issue by removing the pattern from the default JSON schema entirely (reverting to v2.11 output), then adds an opt-in `get_decimal_pattern()` hook plus a ~150-line `build_decimal_pattern` implementation with hand-rolled regex generators (`_repeat`, `_int_range_pattern`, separate validation/serialization builders, inf/NaN handling). This is a product decision and a substantial redesign well beyond the issue's ask: it silently drops a documented v2.12 feature for all users who relied on `max_digits`/`decimal_places` appearing as a pattern, and introduces a large amount of intricate regex-construction code whose correctness is hard to verify by inspection (enumerating whole-part widths, exponent range patterns, decimal_places > max_digits handling). The tests are extensive, but the volume of new logic is itself risk, and it is not required to fix the reported bug. Under the scope rule, this extra work earns no credit and counts against B where it adds risk and changes default behavior.

A is a correct, minimal, well-tested fix at the point the issue identifies; B fixes the symptom by removing the feature and bundles a risky redesign. A is the better fix.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

**`model_json_schema(mode="serialization")` pattern for `Decimal` breaks on scientific notation**

The serialization schema for `Decimal` fields generates a regex that rejects values that `model_dump_json()` itself produces.

Specifically: `pydantic-core`'s serializer calls `str()` on `Decimal` objects, which outputs scientific notation for small/large values. E.g. `Decimal('0.0000001')` becomes `"1E-7"`. But the pattern added in #11987 (`^(?!^[-+.]*$)[+-]?0*\d*\.?\d*$`) has no `[eE]` component, so it'll never match those strings.

As a result, any downstream consumer validating `model_dump_json()` output against `model_json_schema()`, such as OpenAPI validators and codegen + validation tools like Orval + Zod, will intermittently reject perfectly valid serialized values. Intermittent because only certain `Decimal` values trigger scientific notation.

**v2.11**:
```json
{"anyOf": [{"type": "string"}, {"type": "null"}]}
```

**v2.12**:
```json
{"anyOf": [{"pattern": "^(?!^[-+.]*$)[+-]?0*\\d*\\.?\\d*$", "type": "string"}, {"type": "null"}]}
```

Two possible fixes:
- Append `(?:[eE][+-]?\d+)?` to the pattern in serialization mode
- Normalize `Decimal` to fixed-point during serialization before it ever hits the schema

### Example Code

```Python
import json
import re
from decimal import Decimal
from pydantic import BaseModel

class MyModel(BaseModel):
    value: Decimal | None

schema = MyModel.model_json_schema(mode="serialization")
pattern = next(
    v for v in schema["properties"]["value"]["anyOf"] if v.get("type") == "string"
)["pattern"]
regex = re.compile(pattern)

# pydantic serializes this as "1E-7" which fails its own schema's pattern
m = MyModel(value=Decimal("0.0000001"))
serialized = json.loads(m.model_dump_json())["value"]

print(f"Pattern: {pattern}")
print(f"Serialized: {serialized!r}")
print(f"Matches: {bool(regex.match(serialized))}")
# Pattern: ^(?!^[-+.]*$)[+-]?0*\d*\.?\d*$
# Serialized: '1E-7'
# Matches: False
```

+    # e.g. Infinity, inf, NaN, sNaN, NaN123 (case-insensitive). Spelled out explicitly, as inline flags
+    # aren't supported by all regular expression engines:
+    non_finite = r'|[iI][nN][fF](?:[iI][nN][iI][tT][yY])?|[sS]?[nN][aA][nN][0-9]*' if allow_inf_nan else ''
+    if max_digits is None and decimal_places is None:
+        return rf'^[+-]?(?:{number}(?:{exponent})?{non_finite})$'
+
+    alts: list[str] = []
+    if max_digits is not None and decimal_places is not None:
+        # If `decimal_places > max_digits`, no whole digits are allowed and `max_digits` bounds the decimal places:
+        whole = max(0, max_digits - decimal_places)
+        places = min(max_digits, decimal_places)
+        int_part = f'0*{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, whole)}' if whole else '0+'
+        opt_int_part = f'0*{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, whole)}'
+        opt_frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, places)}0*'
+        frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, places)}0*' if places else r'\.0+'
+        alts += [f'{int_part}(?:{opt_frac_part})?', f'{opt_int_part}{frac_part}']
+    elif max_digits is not None:
+        # The whole part and decimal part must have at most `max_digits` digits in total,
+        # so we enumerate the possible widths of the whole part:
+        int_part = f'0*{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, max_digits)}' if max_digits else '0+'
+        alts.append(rf'{int_part}(?:\.0*)?')
+        alts += [
+            rf'0*{_repeat("[0-9]", whole, whole)}\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, max_digits - whole)}0*'
+            for whole in range(max_digits)
+        ] or [r'0*\.0+']
+    else:
+        assert decimal_places is not None
+        opt_frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, decimal_places)}0*'
+        frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, decimal_places)}0*' if decimal_places else r'\.0+'
+        alts += [f'[0-9]+(?:{opt_frac_part})?', f'[0-9]*{frac_part}']
+
+    alts.append(f'{number}{exponent}')
+    return rf'^[+-]?(?:{"|".join(alts)}{non_finite})$'
+
+
+def _decimal_serialization_pattern(max_digits: int | None, decimal_places: int | None, allow_inf_nan: bool) -> str:
+    """Build the decimal pattern for the `'serialization'` mode.
+
+    Decimals are serialized using `str()`, producing either:
+
+    - The plain notation (`'123.45'`), when the exponent is lower than or equal to 0 and the adjusted
+      exponent is greater than or equal to -6.
+    - The scientific notation otherwise (`'1E+3'`, `'1.5E-7'`, `'0E-10'`), with a single digit before
+      the optional decimal point and an always signed exponent.
+
+    Trailing zeros of the decimal part are preserved by `str()`, but aren't counted by the validation logic.
+    """
+
+    def frac_part(places: int) -> str:
+        return rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, places)}0*' if places else r'\.0+'
+
+    alts: list[str] = []
+
+    # Plain notation:
+    if max_digits is not None and decimal_places is not None:
+        whole = max(0, max_digits - decimal_places)
+        places = min(max_digits, decimal_places)
+        int_part = f'(?:0|[1-9]{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, whole - 1)})' if whole else '0'
+        alts.append(f'{int_part}(?:{frac_part(places)})?')
+    elif max_digits is not None:
+        # The whole part and decimal part must have at most `max_digits` digits in total,
+        # so we enumerate the possible widths of the whole part:
+        alts.append(rf'0(?:\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, max_digits)}0*)?')
+        alts += [
+            f'[1-9]{_repeat("[0-9]", whole - 1, whole - 1)}(?:{frac_part(max_digits - whole)})?'
+            for whole in range(1, max_digits + 1)
+        ]
+    elif decimal_places is not None:
+        alts.append(f'(?:0|[1-9][0-9]*)(?:{frac_part(decimal_places)})?')
+    else:
+        alts.append(r'(?:0|[1-9][0-9]*)(?:\.[0-9]+)?')
+
+    # Zero with an exponent (e.g. `'0E-10'`), which normalizes to zero and thus satisfies any constraint:
+    alts.append(r'0E[+-][1-9][0-9]*')
+
+    # Scientific notation with a positive exponent `k` (e.g. `'1.5E+3'`): the value has `k + 1` whole digits
+    # and no decimal places:
+    if max_digits is None:
+        alts.append(r'[1-9](?:\.[0-9]+)?E\+[1-9][0-9]*')
+    else:
+        max_exponent = max_digits - (decimal_places or 0) - 1
+        if max_exponent >= 1:
+            alts.append(rf'[1-9](?:\.[0-9]+)?E\+{_int_range_pattern(max_exponent)}')
+
+    # Scientific notation with a negative exponent `k` (`k >= 7`, e.g. `'1.5E-7'`): the value has no whole digits,
+    # and `k` + (the number of significant decimal digits of the coefficient) decimal places:
+    if max_digits is None and decimal_places is None:
+        alts.append(r'[1-9](?:\.[0-9]+)?E-[1-9][0-9]*')
+    else:
+        max_places = min(c for c in (max_digits, decimal_places) if c is not None)
+        alts += [f'[1-9](?:{frac_part(max_places - k)})?E-{k}' for k in range(7, max_places + 1)]
+
+    if allow_inf_nan:
+        # `str()` produces `'Infinity'`, `'NaN'` and `'sNaN'` (with an optional payload):
+        alts += ['Infinity', 's?NaN[0-9]*']
+
+    return rf'^-?(?:{"|".join(alts)})$'
 
 
 def _deduplicate_schemas(schemas: Iterable[JsonDict]) -> list[JsonDict]:
     return list({_make_json_hashable(schema): schema for schema in schemas}.values())
 
 
+_HashableJsonValue: TypeAlias = (

+)
+
+

     if isinstance(value, dict):

title: Cannot use `None` as type argument

judge.reasoning: Both patches widen the `__class_getitem__` annotation so `None` and other special forms are accepted, but they differ sharply in robustness, tests, and scope. Patch B replaces `type[Any] | tuple[type[Any], ...]` with `Any` (plus `model_parametrized_name` to `tuple[Any, ...]`), with a comment explaining why. `Any` is understood by every type checker, including PyCharm, which is the checker named in the issue. Patch B also adds targeted typechecking tests that exercise exactly the reported scenarios: `__class_getitem__(None)`, `Literal[1]`, `int | None`, a tuple containing `None`, and `model_parametrized_name` with special forms. These would fail on the old annotation and pass after the change. Patch A instead performs a repository-wide migration to PEP 747 `TypeForm`, touching decorators, fields, pipeline, serializers, validators, TypeAdapter (removing its overloads and a documented mypy workaround), `create_model`, CI (pinning a pyright version with a comment implying a regression), the Makefile, and adding pyrefly configuration and dozens of `# pyrefly: ignore` comments. None of its test changes cover `Box[None]` or `__class_getitem__` with `None`; the new `type_form.py` tests `create_model`, `ValidateAs`, and `field_serializer`, not the issue. Relying on `TypeForm` is also riskier for the reported case: TypeForm support is still partial or absent in several checkers (the patch itself has to pin pyright and carve out mypy/pyrefly exceptions for sentinels), and PyCharm, the reporter's tool, has no guarantee of understanding `TypeForm[Any]`, so the original warning may persist. The sweeping unrelated changes add review burden and regression risk without improving the fix for this issue. Patch B resolves the issue directly, tests it, and stays in scope.

Pydantic's BaseModel.__class_getitem__ is annotated as `typevar_values: type[Any] | tuple[type[Any], ...]`, which causes type checkers to reject `None` as a type argument even though `None` is a valid PEP 484 type
annotation meaning `type(None)` / `NoneType`.

Error in PyCharm: `Expected type 'type | tuple[type, ...]', got 'type[None]'`

Root cause: pydantic/main.py BaseModel.__class_getitem__ signature should accept
`None` (and other special forms) as valid type arguments, not just `type[Any]`.

We could use `NoneType` to get rid of the problem, however, I suggest we update annotation on pydantic side.

### Example Code

```Python
import pydantic as p


class Box[T](p.BaseModel):
    pass


# Triggers the warning because Pydantic's __class_getitem__ is typed as
# typevar_values: type[Any] | tuple[type[Any], ...]
# and None is not type[Any]:
x = Box[None]()
```

title: RootModel.model_dump() typing signature rejects supported serialization arguments

judge.reasoning: Both patches make the identical signature change (IncEx include/exclude, context: Any | None, add fallback and polymorphic_serialization in the right positions), so correctness is equal and the independent tests confirm it. The difference is in tests and scope. Patch A adds exactly what the issue asks for: type-checking regression cases in tests/typechecking/root_model.py exercising the three failing calls (context='prefix', fallback=, polymorphic_serialization=) with assert_type(..., Any), which fail under mypy/pyright before the fix and pass after, plus a small runtime test. Patch B adds a clever runtime sync test that re-executes root_model.py with typing.TYPE_CHECKING monkeypatched to True and compares inspect signatures; it does fail before the fix and would catch future drift, but it is hacky (global mutation of typing.TYPE_CHECKING, re-importing the module under a fake name) and adds no type-checker-level test, which is the actual surface the issue is about. B also replaces the concise 'see BaseModel.model_dump' docstring with a ~40-line verbatim copy of the BaseModel docstring, which is unrelated churn, introduces text that is wrong for RootModel ('Generate a dictionary representation', 'Returns: A dictionary representation') while the method is annotated Any, and relies on the new test to keep two copies in sync. A is tighter, lands tests where the issue specifies, and carries less risk; B's extra work earns no credit and slightly obscures the fix.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

`RootModel` inherits the runtime implementation of `BaseModel.model_dump()`, but defines a separate declaration under `TYPE_CHECKING` to preserve its more precise return type.

That declaration has diverged from the base method:

- `context` is restricted to `dict[str, Any] | None` instead of `Any | None`.
- `fallback` is missing.
- `polymorphic_serialization` is missing.

As a result, Mypy, Pyright, and Pyrefly reject valid calls that succeed at runtime.

All three calls in the example below succeed at runtime.

Mypy currently reports errors equivalent to:

```text
Argument "context" to "model_dump" of "RootModel" has incompatible type "str"
Unexpected keyword argument "fallback" for "model_dump" of "RootModel"
Unexpected keyword argument "polymorphic_serialization" for "model_dump" of "RootModel"
```

Pyright and Pyrefly report the same signature incompatibilities.

## Expected behavior

The type-checking-only `RootModel.model_dump()` declaration should accept the same parameters, annotations, defaults, and ordering as `BaseModel.model_dump()`, while preserving the more precise `RootModel` return annotation.

## Cause

The declaration appears to have drifted as the base method evolved:

- Serialization context originally updated both signatures.
- `BaseModel.context` was later widened to `Any`.
- `fallback` was subsequently added to `BaseModel.model_dump()`.
- `polymorphic_serialization` was later added to `BaseModel.model_dump()`.

Those later changes were not propagated to the manually maintained `RootModel` declaration.

## Proposed fix

Update only the static `RootModel.model_dump()` signature and add focused regression cases to `tests/typechecking/root_model.py`.

No runtime serialization behavior needs to change.

I have prepared and locally validated a focused two-file fix. The following checks pass:

- Mypy type-checking suite
- Pyright type-checking suite
- Pyrefly type-checking suite
- Focused RootModel serialization tests
- Ruff lint and formatting checks
- `git diff --check`

I would be happy to submit the PR after the issue is reviewed and assigned.

### Example Code

```Python
from typing import Any

from pydantic import BaseModel, RootModel, SerializationInfo, model_serializer


class ContextRoot(RootModel[str]):
    @model_serializer
    def serialize_root(self, info: SerializationInfo) -> str:
        return f'{info.context}:{self.root}'


class Unknown:
    pass


class Base(BaseModel):
    x: int


class Sub(Base):
    y: int


ContextRoot(root='value').model_dump(context='prefix')

RootModel[Any](root=Unknown()).model_dump(
    mode='json',
    fallback=lambda _: 'fallback',
)

RootModel[list[Base]](root=[Sub(x=1, y=2)]).model_dump(
    polymorphic_serialization=True,
)
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```Text

        pydantic-core version: 2.47.0
          pydantic-core build: profile=debug pgo=false
               python version: 3.13.5 | packaged by Anaconda, Inc. | (main, Jun 12 2025, 11:23:37) [Clang 14.0.6 ]
                     platform: macOS-15.7.3-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O

```

title: Unexpected serialization schema with `ValidateAs`

judge.reasoning: Both patches share the same core fix: build the serializer from `handler(source)` (falling back to `any_schema()` on GENERATE_SCHEMA_ERRORS) and attach it via a wrap serializer, so the validated `int` is no longer serialized as `list[int]`. Independent tests confirm both resolve the reported warning. Patch B goes further on correctness in two ways that matter for the same field: (1) it adds a `pydantic_js_annotation_functions` hook so `model_json_schema(mode='serialization')` reports the source type (`integer`) rather than falling through to the inner `list[int]` schema, which is what Patch A would produce since `GenerateJsonSchema.ser_schema` ignores a function-wrap ser schema without `return_schema`; (2) it handles the `is-instance` schema produced under `arbitrary_types_allowed`, where the serializer should infer and JSON schema generation would otherwise fail. Patch B's tests are also stronger: they use `warnings.simplefilter('error')` so the regression would fail loudly, and they cover the issue example, a model source type, a custom serializer composed with ValidateAs, arbitrary source types with and without `arbitrary_types_allowed`, and both JSON schema modes. Patch A's tests only check `model_dump_json` output without asserting the warning is gone, and it incidentally renames an existing test. Patch A leaves a TODO comment rather than addressing the JSON schema consequence. B's extra scope is tightly related to the fix and adds little risk.

### Initial Checks

### Description

From https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/discussions/13232:

```python
import pydantic as p
import typing as t

def first_even(nums: list[int]) -> int:

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make `EllipsisType` fields work in Python mode, and the independent tests pass identically. The difference is in how each handles the parts the issue does not specify (JSON, JSON schema) and in consistency with the codebase.

Patch A adds a first-class `ellipsis` core schema in pydantic-core, mirroring the existing `missing-sentinel` validator/serializer almost line for line (LazyLock singleton, `impl_py_gc_traverse!`, registered in `CombinedValidator`/`CombinedSerializer`, a registered `ellipsis_error` with a message in the error table, `EllipsisSchema` + `ellipsis_schema()` in `core_schema.py`, and a `GenerateJsonSchema.ellipsis_schema` hook that raises `PydanticInvalidForJsonSchema`). The validator uses `input.as_python()` and an identity check against `PyEllipsis`, so it is strict and correct; JSON validation and JSON serialization fail loudly rather than inventing a representation. Tests cover the error registry, the schema function table, JSON-schema rejection, and TypeAdapter validate/dump/dump_json behaviour. Model-level tests are thin, which is a weakness, and the diff is larger because it spans Rust and Python, but the extra scope is the conventional way this repo adds a standard-library singleton type.

Patch B is a pure-Python plain validator function plus a `when_used='json'` serializer that maps Ellipsis to the string `"..."` in both directions, with a `const` JSON schema. It has broader model-level tests and docs. However it introduces an undocumented-in-the-issue lossy JSON convention that creates real ambiguity: in a union like `EllipsisType | str` (or `str | EllipsisType`) the JSON string `"..."` validates to different Python values depending on member order, and a genuine `'...'` string cannot round-trip distinctly from Ellipsis. Its own test shows the awkward error location `('subset', 1, 'function-plain[ellipsis_validator()]')` leaking into user-facing errors, and it uses an ad-hoc `PydanticCustomError('ellipsis_required', ...)` rather than a registered error type, unlike how `NoneType`/`MISSING` are handled.

On correctness A is strictly faithful to the type with no surprising semantics; on craft A follows the surrounding conventions closely; B wins on breadth of tests and docs but that is outweighed by the design risk of its JSON mapping. A is the better fix.

### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/get-started/) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

`Ellipsis` is a builtin type that `pydantic` does not support. Its usage is infrequent, but it can be useful to express placeholders:

This is a bit of a contrived example, but:
```python
class Model(pydantic.BaseModel):
    m: list[list[float]]
    subset: tuple[int | Ellipsis, int | Ellipsis]

    def subset_arr(self) -> np.NDArray:
        return np.asarray(self.m)[*self.subset]
```

Here's how I implement this right now with an adapter: https://github.com/psalvaggio/scientific_pydantic/blob/main/src/scientific_pydantic/ellipsis.py

However, since this is a standard library type, I think this would be a good thing to live in `pydantic` itself.

+// This serializer is defined so that building a schema serializer containing an
+// 'ellipsis' core schema doesn't crash. In practice, the serializer can be used
+// if the 'ellipsis' core schema is used standalone (e.g. with a Pydantic type
+// adapter), but this isn't something we explicitly support.
+
+use std::borrow::Cow;
+use std::sync::{Arc, LazyLock};
+
+use pyo3::prelude::*;
+use pyo3::types::{PyDict, PyEllipsis};
+
+use serde::ser::Error;
+
+use crate::PydanticSerializationUnexpectedValue;
+use crate::definitions::DefinitionsBuilder;
+use crate::serializers::SerializationState;
+
+use super::{BuildSerializer, CombinedSerializer, TypeSerializer};
+
+#[derive(Debug)]
+pub struct EllipsisSerializer {}
+
+static ELLIPSIS_SERIALIZER: LazyLock<Arc<CombinedSerializer>> =
+    LazyLock::new(|| Arc::new(EllipsisSerializer {}.into()));
+
+impl BuildSerializer for EllipsisSerializer {
+    const EXPECTED_TYPE: &'static str = "ellipsis";
+
+    fn build(
+        _schema: &Bound<'_, PyDict>,
+        _config: Option<&Bound<'_, PyDict>>,
+        _definitions: &mut DefinitionsBuilder<Arc<CombinedSerializer>>,
+    ) -> PyResult<Arc<CombinedSerializer>> {
+        Ok(ELLIPSIS_SERIALIZER.clone())
+    }
+}
+
+impl_py_gc_traverse!(EllipsisSerializer {});
+
+impl TypeSerializer for EllipsisSerializer {
+    fn to_python(&self, value: &Bound<'_, PyAny>, _state: &mut SerializationState<'_>) -> PyResult<Py<PyAny>> {
+        let ellipsis = PyEllipsis::get(value.py());
+
+        if value.is(ellipsis) {
+            Ok(ellipsis.to_owned().into_any().unbind())
+        } else {
+            Err(
+                PydanticSerializationUnexpectedValue::new_from_msg(Some("Expected 'Ellipsis' object".to_string()))
+                    .to_py_err(),
+            )
+        }
+    }
+
+    fn json_key<'a, 'py>(
+        &self,
+        key: &'a Bound<'py, PyAny>,
+        state: &mut SerializationState<'py>,
+    ) -> PyResult<Cow<'a, str>> {
+        self.invalid_as_json_key(key, state, Self::EXPECTED_TYPE)
+    }
+
+    fn serde_serialize<S: serde::ser::Serializer>(
+        &self,
+        _value: &Bound<'_, PyAny>,
+        _serializer: S,
+        _state: &mut SerializationState<'_>,
+    ) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error> {
+        Err(Error::custom("'Ellipsis' can't be serialized to JSON".to_string()))
+    }
+
+    fn get_name(&self) -> &str {
+        Self::EXPECTED_TYPE
+    }
+}

title: Allow arbitrary core schemas for serialization

judge.reasoning:
Both patches give pydantic-core a way to say "serialize with this core schema", but they differ in design and completeness.

Patch A changes the Rust fallthrough to `Self::build(&ser_schema)` and widens `SerSchema` to include `CoreSchema` (via a string-typed alias plus `Union[...]  # noqa` workarounds). That lets a core schema be passed directly, which is why the four independent tests that pass a raw schema as `serialization` pass only with A. However, A has real gaps: (1) it does not touch `self_schema.py`, so `validate_core_schema` would still reject a raw core schema in `serialization`; (2) the design is ambiguous for `function-plain`/`function-wrap` validator schemas (they collide with the ser-function schemas), which A papers over with a new `as_ser_schema` helper that is tested but never used; (3) it leaves every identity-wrap workaround in pydantic in place and merely rewrites the `ValidateAs` TODO instead of resolving it. The issue is explicitly framed around that TODO and the workaround sites, and the one independent test checking that `ValidateAs` no longer goes through `FunctionWrap` fails on A.

Patch B adds an explicit `SchemaSerSchema` (`type: 'schema'`) with a `schema_ser_schema()` helper, a dedicated Rust arm that builds a full serializer from the inner schema (so nested `serialization`, definitions, recursion, models, dataclasses all work, as its core tests show), updates the self-schema so schema validation accepts it, handles the new type in `GenerateJsonSchema.ser_schema`, and migrates all workaround sites (`ValidateAs`, `PlainValidator`, `SkipValidation`, `InstanceOf`, non-dict Mapping) with pydantic-level tests asserting the wrap serializer is gone and filtering/json-schema still work. It avoids the function-schema ambiguity entirely. The issue text itself points at the missing piece as a `SerSchema` member that "takes a schema", which is exactly what B adds; the four independent tests B fails do so only because they assume the raw-schema API shape, not because the capability is missing.

On correctness B is complete end-to-end and consistent with self-schema validation; A delivers the core capability with typing hacks, an unused helper, and no caller migration. On tests both are solid, B's cover more real scenarios. On craft B is cleaner and follows existing `SerSchema` conventions. B wins.

issue_md:
As per the TODO in https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/13487:

There is currently no way to tell `pydantic-core` "serialize this value using this core schema". `Ser`Schema is:

```python
SerSchema = Union[
    SimpleSerSchema,
    PlainSerializerFunctionSerSchema,
    WrapSerializerFunctionSerSchema,
    FormatSerSchema,
    ToStringSerSchema,
    ModelSerSchema,
]
```

The only member that expresses "use this schema" is `SimpleSerSchema`, and it does not take a schema at all, only a name from a closed literal:

```python
ExpectedSerializationTypes = Literal[
    'none', 'int', 'bool', 'float', 'str', 'bytes', 'bytearray', 'list', 'tuple',
    'set', 'frozenset', 'generator', 'dict', 'datetime', 'date', 'time', 'timedelta',
    'url', 'multi-host-url', 'json', 'uuid', 'any',
]

class SimpleSerSchema(TypedDict, total=False):
    type: Required[ExpectedSerializationTypes]
```

So an arbitrary schema (a model, a dataclass, `list[int]`, a TypedDict, anything constructed by the schema generator) cannot be used directly. Every place in Pydantic that needs it works around the gap the same way: it wraps the schema in a wrap serializer whose function is the identity, purely so the schema can ride along in the `schema` argument.

From `ValidateAs.__get_pydantic_core_schema__()`:

https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/27f95c789b20aa23306e5ce559327db0e9a10a6e/pydantic/functional_validators.py#L911-L917

patches.ours:

@@ -476,6 +476,36 @@ def model_ser_schema(cls: type[Any], schema: CoreSchema) -> ModelSerSchema:
     return ModelSerSchema(type='model', cls=cls, schema=schema)
 
 
+class SchemaSerSchema(TypedDict, total=False):
+    type: Required[Literal['schema']]
+    schema: Required[CoreSchema]
+
+
+def schema_ser_schema(schema: CoreSchema) -> SchemaSerSchema:
+    """
+    Returns a schema for serialization using an arbitrary core schema.
+
+    The value is serialized as if it was validated by `schema`, regardless of the
+    schema it is attached to:
+
+    ```py
+    from pydantic_core import SchemaSerializer, core_schema
+
+    schema = core_schema.any_schema(
+        serialization=core_schema.schema_ser_schema(
+            core_schema.list_schema(core_schema.int_schema())
+        )
+    )
+    s = SchemaSerializer(schema)
+    assert s.to_json([1, 2]) == b'[1,2]'
+    ```
+
+    Args:
+        schema: The core schema to use to serialize the value
+    """
+    return SchemaSerSchema(type='schema', schema=schema)
+
+

     | PlainSerializerFunctionSerSchema

+"""Tests for arbitrary core schemas being used as the `serialization` schema."""

+        (core_schema.simple_ser_schema('list'), [1, 'a'], [1, 'a'], b'[1,"a"]'),
+        (core_schema.list_schema(core_schema.int_schema()), [1, 2], [1, 2], b'[1,2]'),
+        (
+            core_schema.tuple_schema([core_schema.int_schema(), core_schema.str_schema()]),
+            (1, 'a'),
+            (1, 'a'),
+            b'[1,"a"]',
+        ),
+        (
+            core_schema.dict_schema(core_schema.str_schema(), core_schema.int_schema()),
+            {'a': 1},
+            {'a': 1},
+            b'{"a":1}',
+        ),
+        (
+            core_schema.typed_dict_schema({'a': core_schema.typed_dict_field(core_schema.int_schema())}),
+            {'a': 1, 'b': 2},
+            {'a': 1},
+            b'{"a":1}',
+        ),
+        (
+            core_schema.definitions_schema(
+                core_schema.definition_reference_schema('list_of_int'),
+                [core_schema.list_schema(core_schema.int_schema(), ref='list_of_int')],
+            ),
+            [1, 2],
+            [1, 2],
+            b'[1,2]',
+        ),
+        # `'function-before'`/`'function-after'` core schemas serialize using the inner schema:
+        (
+            core_schema.no_info_after_validator_function(lambda v: v, core_schema.int_schema()),
+            1,
+            1,
+            b'1',
+        ),
+    ],
+)

+    s = SchemaSerializer(core_schema.any_schema(serialization=ser_schema))

title: model_dump(exclude=...) is silently ignored in python mode when a wrap model_serializer is gated with when_used="json"

judge.reasoning: Both patches target the same root cause in the function_type_serializer macro: when `self.call` reports the function was skipped by the `when_used` gate (the `Ok((false, v))` arm), the fallback serializer was being run with include/exclude scoped to empty, so the caller's filtering vanished. Patch A short-circuits with an early return that leaves the existing state untouched; Patch B threads the choice of IncludeExclude through the match and scopes to either empty or a clone of the current state. Functionally they are equivalent across to_python, json_key and serde_serialize, and the independent tests confirm both fix the issue, including nested excludes and include. B's single-path approach is marginally more compact, but it adds a new public clone-returning accessor on SerializationState and re-scopes the state to the same value it already holds, which is slightly redundant; A's early return is a touch repetitive across three methods but avoids any clone and does not touch extra.rs. On craft the two are close. The deciding difference is tests: A adds a pydantic-core level test (plain and wrap, both json and json-unless-none, exercising include and exclude on a dict schema) plus pydantic tests for model_serializer, field_serializer with nested exclude, and a nested model case, each cross-checked against JSON mode. B adds one test covering plain and wrap with when_used='json' only, with no json-unless-none coverage and no nested or field-serializer coverage. A's tests more completely pin the behaviour the issue asks for and would catch regressions in more of the affected paths, so A is the better patch overall.

title: Cannot create `defauldict` field with `dict` value type

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the root cause identically: `dict` (and `frozenset`) were missing from the allowed-default-types table in `get_defaultdict_default_default_factory`, and both add them. All three independent tests pass on both. The difference is in risk and scope. Patch A adds a speculative `if sys.version_info >= (3, 15):` block at module import time that references a bare `frozendict` name with `# noqa: F821` (and does the same in the test file). There is no `frozendict` builtin in any released Python, so if that branch ever executes it raises NameError at import of `pydantic._internal._validators`, breaking the entire library on that interpreter. It also silently remaps `collections.abc.Mapping` to `frozendict`, which would change existing behaviour and produce immutable defaults inside a defaultdict, which is semantically odd. None of this is asked for by the issue; it is unrelated churn that adds real risk and obscures the two-line fix. Patch A does include a nice correction of the error message from 'keys' to 'values', and its parametrized test table is reasonable, but it also deletes the existing tests rather than extending them. Patch B is the minimal correct change, keeps existing tests, and adds focused new tests covering bare and parametrized `dict`/`frozenset` plus the exact BaseModel scenario from the issue, asserting the inferred factory and missing-key behaviour. Those tests fail before and pass after. B wins on scope and craft with equal correctness.

title: Memory leak: transient models using Enum methods or Field(exclude_if=...) survive GC

judge.reasoning: Both patches apply the same three root-cause fixes the issue identifies (traverse SerField.serialization_exclude_if, EnumSerializer.class, and EnumValidator.lookup for all four enum validator variants), and both pass every independent test. The differences are in completeness, tests, and churn. Patch A also traverses ComputedField.serialization_exclude_if, which is the same bug class for computed_field(exclude_if=...) and squarely within the issue's 'Field(exclude_if=...)' ask, and makes LiteralLookup traverse expected_py_values and expected_py_primitives so the lookup edge is actually complete rather than only covering the hashable-dict case. Patch A's tests are stronger: a parametrized pydantic-core test over plain/int/str/float enums for both validator and serializer, an exclude_if test across model/typed_dict/dataclass/computed fields, and a pydantic-level test in tests/test_main.py that reproduces the issue's exact transient-module scenario (including the computed-field variant). Patch B's three new tests are valid and would fail before the fix, but B also makes unrelated and risky edits to existing tests: it removes the free-threaded xfail markers and the is_free_threaded import from test_gc_schema_serializer/validator, renames dunder attributes in those tests, and converts comments to docstrings. Dropping those xfails can turn existing passing-as-xfail runs into hard failures on free-threaded builds, and B's new GC tests also omit that marker. That churn obscures the fix and adds risk without addressing the issue. A is more correct at the edges, better tested, and cleaner in scope.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Transient `BaseModel` classes are not collected when either:
* A model field references an `Enum` whose class defines a Python method.
* A model field uses `Field(exclude_if=<Python callable>)`.

After the defining module is removed from `sys.modules` and every ordinary strong reference is dropped, weak references to the model and enum classes remain alive after repeated full `gc.collect()` calls. Repeating this construction in disposable module namespaces causes linear memory growth.

Controls using an enum without methods or a field without `exclude_if` are collected normally.

I encountered this in combination with a Temporal workflow sandbox. With a large interconnected model graph and high volume Temporal workflows this can result in multi-GiB process growth relatively quickly.

The likely cause is missing `PyGcTraverse` edges for Python objects held by pydantic-core:
* `SerField` owns `serialization_exclude_if`, but traverses only `serializer`: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c/pydantic-core/src/serializers/fields.rs#L26-L38
* `EnumSerializer` owns `class`, but traverses only `serializer`: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c/pydantic-core/src/serializers/type_serializers/enum_.rs
* Each `EnumValidator<T>` owns `lookup`, but traverses only `class` and `missing`: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c/pydantic-core/src/validators/enum_.rs

Traversing `py_schema` does not compensate for another unreported direct reference: CPython’s collector accounts for every actual strong edge individually.

I tested a temporary build from Pydantic `main` at `c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c`. Adding only these traversal edges made all objects in the reproduction collectible:
* Add `serialization_exclude_if` to `SerField` traversal.
* Add `class` to `EnumSerializer` traversal.
* Add `lookup` to every `EnumValidator<T>` traversal.

For the enum case, changing only the serializer or only the validator was insufficient; both missing edges were required.

This appears related to earlier missing-traversal fixes such as:

* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/5136
* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/787
* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/1100

I would be happy to submit a focused patch.

(please note that this analysis was LLM assisted)

### Example Code

```Python
import gc
import sys
import types
import weakref

def transient_module(name, source, class_names):
    module = types.ModuleType(name)
    sys.modules[name] = module
    exec(compile(source, f"<{name}>", "exec"), module.__dict__)
    refs = tuple(
        weakref.ref(module.__dict__[class_name])
        for class_name in class_names
    )
    del sys.modules[name]
    del module
    return refs

enum_ref, enum_model_ref = transient_module(
    "_pydantic_enum_gc_repro",
    """
from enum import Enum
from pydantic import BaseModel
class Membership(str, Enum):
    FULL = "full"
    def label(self) -> str:
        return self.value
class Model(BaseModel):
    membership: Membership
""",
    ("Membership", "Model"),
)

(exclude_if_model_ref,) = transient_module(
    "_pydantic_exclude_if_gc_repro",
    """
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
class Model(BaseModel):
    value: int = Field(exclude_if=lambda value: False)
""",
    ("Model",),
)

for _ in range(5):
    gc.collect()

# All three should be False because no intentional strong references remain.
print("enum alive:", enum_ref() is not None)
print("enum model alive:", enum_model_ref() is not None)
print("exclude_if model alive:", exclude_if_model_ref() is not None)

title: TypeError: unhashable type: 'list' in match_type for PEP 695 aliases with a ParamSpec (regression in 2.14.0b1)

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the crash at the exact site the issue identifies, and all six independent tests pass on both. They differ in how they get there and in test quality.

Patch B wraps the `DEPRECATED_ALIASES.get(obj)` lookup in `try/except TypeError`, exactly one of the two fixes the issue proposes. It is self-contained, needs no dependency change, and its comment explains the unhashable case. Its tests target the reported scenario directly: a `TypeAliasType` with a `ParamSpec` parameterized as `[[], int]` (asserting the alias really is unhashable), the same alias inside an optional model field and a `TypeAdapter`, a `Callable[P, R]` alias that validates callables and rejects non-callables, and a `create_module` test using the literal PEP 695 `type Alias[**P, R] = Any` statement from the report. These would fail on base with the reported TypeError and pass after.

Patch A switches to an identity-based lookup, `DEPRECATED_ALIASES_IDS.get(id(obj))`, which depends on a new attribute from typing-inspection and so bumps the minimum dependency from 0.4.2 to 0.4.4. Functionally this is sound (the deprecated aliases are module-level singletons, so id lookup is stable), but it couples a one-line bug fix to a hard dependency floor raise that forces downstream upgrades, and I cannot verify from the diff that the attribute exists in that release. Its test (`test_unhasbable_generic_alias`, misspelled) exercises `list[Annotated[int, Meta()]]` with an unhashable metadata object. That does reach the broken lookup on base, so it is a valid regression test, but it does not cover the ParamSpec/PEP 695 alias case the issue is actually about, and it is a single assertion.

On correctness they are equivalent; on tests B is clearly stronger and closer to the issue; on scope B avoids the dependency bump; on craft B's comment and non-typo test names are better. B is the better fix.

issue_md:
Reported downstream in Giskard-AI/giskard#2719 (breaks `import giskard.checks`); repro and analysis below. The report was drafted jointly with @davidberenstein1957, who invited it to be filed upstream as-is.

### Description

`_generate_schema.match_type` added an unguarded dict lookup in 2.14 that assumes the annotation object is hashable. It is not, for a PEP 695 type alias with a `ParamSpec` parameterized by an empty list. Schema building for any model containing such an annotation crashes.

This is a regression: the same code builds fine on 2.13.4.

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Any
from pydantic import BaseModel

type Alias[**P, R] = Any

class M(BaseModel):
    f: Alias[[], int] | None = None
```

Raises immediately at class-definition time:

```
File ".../pydantic/_internal/_generate_schema.py", line 1127, in match_type
    if origin is not None and (aliased_obj := typing_objects.DEPRECATED_ALIASES.get(obj)):
TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
```

### Mechanism

`Alias[[], int]` is a `types.GenericAlias` whose `__args__` is `([], int)`. Hashing the alias hashes that tuple, which contains a `list` — so it is unhashable. The line at `_generate_schema.py:1127`

```python
if origin is not None and (aliased_obj := typing_objects.DEPRECATED_ALIASES.get(obj)):
```

calls `.get(obj)` without checking that `obj` can be hashed. `dict.get` propagates the `TypeError` rather than treating an unhashable key as absent.

### Suggested fix

Guard the lookup, e.g.

```python
if origin is not None and isinstance(obj, Hashable) and (aliased_obj := typing_objects.DEPRECATED_ALIASES.get(obj)):
```

or wrap it in `try/except TypeError`. An unhashable object cannot be a `DEPRECATED_ALIASES` key by construction, so skipping the lookup is always correct.

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

- pydantic 2.14.0b1 (fails) / 2.13.4 (works)
- Python 3.12.13
- Reproduced on Linux and macOS

### Real-world impact

Hit in [giskard-oss](https://github.com/Giskard-AI/giskard-oss), where `type GeneratorType[**P, R, S] = ...` parameterized as `GeneratorType[[], InputType, None]` makes `import giskard.checks` fail outright under 2.14.0b1. Instrumenting `match_type` confirms the offending object:

```
OFFENDING obj  = GeneratorType[[], InputType, None]
OFFENDING type = <class 'types.GenericAlias'>
OFFENDING args = ([], InputType, None)
```

There is no workaround on the library side short of pinning `pydantic<2.14` (done in Giskard-AI/giskard#2752), which is what downstream has had to do.

title: `SerializeAsAny` fails on a deferred model: `TypeError: 'MockValSer' object is not an instance of 'SchemaSerializer'`

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause the same way: when the `__pydantic_serializer__` attribute does not downcast to `SchemaSerializer`, call the mock's `rebuild()` and use the returned serializer. Both route `serialize_pydantic_serializable` and the `PolymorphismTrampoline` through the shared helper, and both stop the trampoline from silently swallowing the cast error and falling back to the parent serializer (A by returning `Option` and propagating `?`, B by a `hasattr` pre-check then `?`). All independent tests pass on both.

The meaningful difference is in how the rebuild resolves forward references. `MockValSer.rebuild()` delegates to `model_rebuild(_parent_namespace_depth=5)`, a frame depth calibrated for the `__getattr__` lazy hook being hit from a Python call site. Patch B calls `rebuild()` with no arguments from Rust, so the namespace used to resolve annotations is whatever frame happens to sit five levels above `model_rebuild` in the serialization call stack (e.g. the caller's caller of `model_dump_json`). That is an arbitrary, call-depth-dependent namespace and can resolve or fail to resolve names depending on where serialization is invoked. Patch A recognises this, adds a `parent_namespace_depth` keyword to `MockValSer.rebuild` and the `attempt_rebuild` handlers, and passes `0` from Rust so no caller frame is used. It also adds `test_serialization_inference_unbuildable_model` to pin that behaviour, and a `create_module` forward-ref test showing module-level resolution still works. B has no equivalent reasoning or test, so its fix is subtly fragile in exactly the scenario the issue describes (a worker process serializing classes it never validated, from an unrelated call stack).

On tests, B is somewhat broader on the issue's literal scenario (python/json modes, `serialize_as_any` flag, `polymorphic_serialization`, and 'not fully defined' error cases on both paths). A covers the flag and polymorphic paths in one parametrized test, the error path via the unbuildable test, and the forward-ref path. Both would fail before and pass after.

Scope: A touches more files (moves `py_get_attrs` to `tools.rs`, adds a `Protocol` type in `_mock_val_ser.py`, and adds an unrelated xfail test in `test_construction.py`). The xfail test is minor churn; the rest is in service of the namespace fix. B is leaner and uses pyo3's `getattr_opt` directly, which is slightly cleaner than A's moved helper. These are small craft points and do not outweigh A's more correct handling of namespace resolution during a Rust-triggered rebuild.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Serialization with `SerializeAsAny` fails when the runtime class of the value is a deferred model.
A deferred model is a model with `defer_build=True` that pydantic did not build yet.
The call raises this error:

```
PydanticSerializationError: Error serializing to JSON: TypeError: 'MockValSer' object is not an instance of 'SchemaSerializer'
```

I expect pydantic to build the deferred model at first use, and then serialize the value.

### Cause

The cause is in pydantic-core, in `src/serializers/infer.rs`.
The function `serialize_pydantic_serializable` reads the attribute `__pydantic_serializer__` from the value.
On a deferred model, this attribute holds a `MockValSer` object, not a `SchemaSerializer` object.
The code downcasts the object to `SchemaSerializer`.
The downcast fails, and the error goes to the caller.

`MockValSer` has a lazy rebuild hook in `__getattr__`.
A Python method call starts this hook.
A Rust downcast does not start this hook.
As a result, the same deferred instance serializes correctly through a direct `model_dump_json()`, but fails through `SerializeAsAny`.
The example code below shows this asymmetry.

### Impact

This failure occurred for us in production.
A worker process serialized instances of model classes that it never validated in that process.
Each `model_dump_json()` call on the parent model failed.

### Versions tested

The failure occurs on all versions that we tested:

- pydantic 2.12.5 / pydantic-core 2.41.5
- pydantic 2.13.4 / pydantic-core 2.46.4
- pydantic 2.14.0b1 / pydantic-core 2.48.0

### Related issues

- #7713 tracks `MockValSer` errors in general.
- #12282 reported this failure and was closed as a duplicate.

### Proposed fix

I have a fix with tests ready on a fork.
The fix changes `get_pydantic_serializer` in `infer.rs`:

1. The function downcasts the attribute value to `SchemaSerializer` as before.
2. If the downcast fails, the function calls the `rebuild()` method of the mock object.
3. The function then uses the serializer that `rebuild()` returns.
4. An object without a `rebuild()` method keeps the current downcast error.

`serialize_pydantic_serializable` and `PolymorphismTrampoline` use the same code path, so one change repairs both.
All pydantic and pydantic-core test suites pass with the fix.
Please assign this issue to me, and I will open the pull request.


### Example Code

```Python
from typing import Optional

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, SerializeAsAny


class Child(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(defer_build=True)
    x: int = 1


class Sub(Child):
    y: int = 2


class Parent(BaseModel):
    content: Optional[SerializeAsAny[Child]] = None


# model_construct() does not validate, so pydantic does not build Sub.
# This is equal to a process that serializes a class that it never validated.
sub = Sub.model_construct(x=1, y=2)
parent = Parent.model_construct(content=sub)
assert Sub.__pydantic_complete__ is False

# 1) The SerializeAsAny path fails on the deferred model.
try:
    parent.model_dump_json()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}")
    # PydanticSerializationError: Error serializing to JSON: TypeError:
    # 'MockValSer' object is not an instance of 'SchemaSerializer'

# 2) The direct Python path rebuilds the same deferred model and succeeds.
print(sub.model_dump_json())  # {"x":1,"y":2}
assert Sub.__pydantic_complete__ is True

# 3) After the rebuild, the SerializeAsAny path also succeeds.
print(parent.model_dump_json())  # {"content":{"x":1,"y":2}}
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```Text
pydantic version: 2.14.0b1
        pydantic-core version: 2.48.0
          pydantic-core build: profile=release pgo=false
               python version: 3.11.15 (main, Mar 25 2026, 02:58:47) [Clang 22.1.1 ]
                     platform: macOS-26.5.2-arm64-arm-64bit
             related packages: typing_extensions-4.16.0
                       commit: unknown

The same example also fails on these versions:
- pydantic 2.13.4 / pydantic-core 2.46.4 (latest stable)
- pydantic 2.12.5 / pydantic-core 2.41.5
```

title: Runtime by_name/by_alias arguments dropped by model_validator(mode="wrap")

judge.reasoning: The Rust change is byte-for-byte equivalent in both patches: InternalValidator gains by_alias/by_name fields captured from the incoming Extra and threads them into the Extra rebuilt in validate() and validate_assignment() instead of hard-coding None. That is the root cause (the wrap handler and generator item validator rebuild Extra and lost the runtime flags), so correctness is equal and all independent tests pass on both. The difference is the tests. Patch B adds a pydantic-core level test in test_function.py that exercises the wrap function validator directly against a typed_dict schema with all four by_alias/by_name combinations, plus a parametrized pydantic-level test covering TypeAdapter, model_validate, model_validate_json, a nested field-level wrap validator, and the Iterable generator path (which uses the same InternalValidator and was also affected). Patch A adds one targeted test for the wrap paths and a second test asserting strict/extra/from_attributes/context forwarding, which already worked before the change and so does not guard the fix. B's tests are more precise about the regression, cover more of the affected entry points, and test at the layer where the code changed. Scope and craft are otherwise equivalent.

title: JSON Schema ignores `ser_json_temporal`, so serialization schemas contradict `model_dump_json()` output

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the root cause the same way: date/time/datetime schemas now consult `ser_json_temporal`, and `timedelta_schema` mirrors pydantic-core by checking for the key's presence in `config_dict` before falling back to `ser_json_timedelta`. All independent tests pass on both, so they are equivalent on the issue's core scenarios. Patch A is slightly cleaner (one `_common_temporal_schema` helper, explicit Literal typing), while B repeats the `in ('seconds', 'milliseconds')` check four times. B pulls ahead on completeness and tests: it also updates `encode_default` so the `to_jsonable_python` fallback (used for stdlib dataclass defaults that bypass the TypeAdapter path) honors `ser_json_temporal` precedence, which is the same schema-vs-dump contradiction the issue describes applied to `default` values, and it adds a test proving the default equals the actual `model_dump_json()` output. B's test matrix is also broader and more discriminating: it covers unset config, `ser_json_temporal` alone, both precedence directions, `ser_json_timedelta` alone (confirming it still only affects timedelta), nested-model config isolation via `$defs`, and defaults under each temporal mode, each asserting against the real dump. A's tests cover the main cases and precedence but not nested config or the default-encoding path. The extra `encode_default` change in B is low risk (it only triggers when `ser_json_temporal` is explicitly set and passes the mode pydantic-core already supports). Net: B is the more thorough fix with stronger tests; A's helper refactor is a minor craft advantage that does not outweigh that.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

`ser_json_temporal` landed in v2.12 and controls how `datetime`, `date`, `time` and `timedelta` are serialized to JSON. `GenerateJsonSchema` was never told about it, so a `mode='serialization'` schema still says these fields are strings even when `model_dump_json()` writes numbers.

With `ser_json_temporal='seconds'` (same with `'milliseconds'`), every temporal field is affected:

```
schema:  {'dt': {'type': 'string', 'format': 'date-time'}, 'td': {'type': 'string', 'format': 'duration'}}
dump:    {'dt': 1577836800.0, 'td': 86400.0}
```

Running that payload through a JSON Schema validator fails with `1577836800.0 is not of type 'string'`, so the schema pydantic publishes rejects the output pydantic itself just produced. `date_schema`, `time_schema` and `datetime_schema` read no config at all right now.

There is a second mismatch that goes the other way, on `timedelta`. `timedelta_schema` only looks at the older `ser_json_timedelta` setting. The docs for `ser_json_temporal` say it takes precedence over `ser_json_timedelta`, and pydantic-core implements exactly that: `SerializationConfig::from_config` and `TimeDeltaSerializer::build` both check whether `ser_json_temporal` is present in the config before falling back to `ser_json_timedelta`. The JSON schema layer does not, so setting `ser_json_temporal='iso8601'` together with `ser_json_timedelta='float'` gives you the reverse problem:

```
schema:  {'td': {'type': 'number'}}
dump:    {'td': 'P1D'}
```

For anyone generating an OpenAPI document from a model this is a silent wrong answer rather than a crash, which is probably why it has gone unnoticed since the setting was added.

I have a patch that mirrors the pydantic-core resolution in the four temporal schema methods, plus tests. Happy to open a PR if you want to assign this to me.

### Example Code

```Python
import json
from datetime import date, datetime, time, timedelta

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict


class Numeric(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(ser_json_temporal='seconds')

    dt: datetime
    d: date
    t: time
    td: timedelta


model = Numeric(dt=datetime(2020, 1, 1), d=date(2020, 1, 1), t=time(12, 0), td=timedelta(days=1))

print(Numeric.model_json_schema(mode='serialization')['properties'])
#> {'dt': {'format': 'date-time', 'title': 'Dt', 'type': 'string'},
#>  'd': {'format': 'date', 'title': 'D', 'type': 'string'},
#>  't': {'format': 'time', 'title': 'T', 'type': 'string'},
#>  'td': {'format': 'duration', 'title': 'Td', 'type': 'string'}}

print(json.loads(model.model_dump_json()))
#> {'dt': 1577836800.0, 'd': 1577836800.0, 't': 43200.0, 'td': 86400.0}


# The timedelta precedence case, wrong in the opposite direction:
class Precedence(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(ser_json_temporal='iso8601', ser_json_timedelta='float')

    td: timedelta


print(Precedence.model_json_schema(mode='serialization')['properties'])
#> {'td': {'title': 'Td', 'type': 'number'}}

print(json.loads(Precedence(td=timedelta(days=1)).model_dump_json()))
#> {'td': 'P1D'}
```
