title: `populate_by_name` (and implicit `validate_by_name` when `validate_by_alias=False`) is ignored by `@validate_call`

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause identified in the issue: the raw `validate_by_name` config key being embedded into `arguments`/`arguments-v3` core schemas, bypassing the compatibility mapping done in `core_config()`. The independent tests confirm both make all seven scenarios pass, including the `validate_by_alias=False` variant.

Patch B's approach of reading the value from `core_config(title=None)` is arguably more elegant because it reuses the single source of truth rather than duplicating the mapping logic. Patch A duplicates that logic in a new `effective_validate_by_name` property, with a docstring explaining it mirrors `core_config()`, which carries a small drift risk but is clearly documented.

Where A pulls ahead is tests and scope discipline. The issue explicitly calls out two behaviours: `populate_by_name=True` and the "worse variant" `validate_by_alias=False`. Patch A adds regression tests for both in `test_validate_call.py` (including asserting the alias is correctly rejected under `validate_by_alias=False`), and parametrizes the experimental arguments-schema test across both `arguments` and `arguments-v3` schema types and all three config spellings. Patch B only tests `populate_by_name` on `validate_call` and only the `arguments-v3` schema type, leaving the `validate_by_alias=False` variant and the legacy `arguments` schema path untested. Patch B also includes unrelated churn, rewriting `dict(...)` to `{...}` in three existing tests, which is noise in a bug-fix diff.

Patch A's extension to model and dataclass signature generation is beyond the issue's ask and earns no credit on its own, but it is low-risk, consistent with the fix, and covered by a new test, so it does not count against it.

On balance A is the better fix due to materially stronger test coverage of the behaviours the issue names, with no unrelated churn.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Since v2.11, `@validate_call(config=ConfigDict(populate_by_name=True))` no longer allows passing an aliased parameter by its name — the same config on a `BaseModel` works, and the [`populate_by_name` docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/config/#pydantic.config.ConfigDict.populate_by_name) say it is strictly equivalent to `validate_by_name=True, validate_by_alias=True` (deprecated in v3, but still supported). Works on 2.10.6; broken on 2.11.x, 2.12.x, and `main`.

A worse variant: `@validate_call(config=ConfigDict(validate_by_alias=False))` makes the aliased parameter impossible to provide at all (both name and alias raise), even though #11503 made `validate_by_alias=False` implicitly enable `validate_by_name`.

Root cause: `_arguments_schema()`/`_arguments_v3_schema()` embed `validate_by_name=self._config_wrapper.validate_by_name` into the core schema (`_generate_schema.py:2081/2149`), reading the raw config key. The backwards-compatibility patch mapping `populate_by_name` → `validate_by_name` only runs inside `ConfigWrapper.core_config()`, and pydantic-core gives the schema-embedded value precedence over the validator config, so the patched core config is never consulted. Models are unaffected because model-fields schemas don't embed the flag.

I have a fix ready and will open a PR.

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import Field, validate_call

@validate_call(config=dict(populate_by_name=True))
def f(a: Annotated[int, Field(alias='b')]) -> int:
    return a

f(b=1)  # OK
f(a=1)  # ValidationError: Unexpected keyword argument
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```text
             pydantic version: 2.14.0b1
        pydantic-core version: 2.48.0
          pydantic-core build: profile=release pgo=false
               python version: 3.11.14 (main, Oct  9 2025, 16:16:55) [Clang 17.0.0 (clang-1700.4.4.1)]
                     platform: macOS-26.5.2-arm64-arm-64bit
             related packages: typing_extensions-4.16.0
                       commit: 2151025
```

(also reproduced on released pydantic 2.11.10 and 2.12.5; not reproducible on 2.10.6)

title: model_dump_json crashes on a SecretStr field with an unvalidated None default (internal AttributeError instead of null/warning)

judge.reasoning: Both patches make the issue's SecretStr example stop raising, and the independent tests do not separate them. The difference is in root cause and robustness. Patch A flips `when_used` to `'unless-none'`, which only skips the custom serializer for the single value `None`; the underlying problem (the serializer dereferences `.get_secret_value()` on whatever it receives) is untouched, so any other mismatched value, e.g. `model_construct(s='hunter2')` or an unvalidated non-secret default, still surfaces an internal AttributeError wrapped in PydanticSerializationError. A also leaves the sibling `_serialize_secret` (generic `Secret[T] = None`) crashing the same way. Patch B addresses the actual cause: it type-checks the value and raises `PydanticSerializationUnexpectedValue`, which is exactly the mechanism pydantic-core uses to emit the standard mismatch UserWarning and fall back to inferred serialization, yielding `null` plus a warning, matching how `int = None` behaves and matching the issue's stated expectation of consistent degrade-gracefully behaviour. It also deliberately omits the secret value from the warning text, with a test asserting the secret does not leak, which is the correct edge handling for this type. Tests: A adds one narrow test that fails before and passes after. B adds parametrized tests across SecretStr, SecretBytes, and Secret[int], covers json, python and mode='json' paths, asserts the warning is emitted, checks Optional still produces no warning, and checks value redaction; these are meaningfully stronger. Scope: B extends the same isinstance-guard pattern to ByteSize, Base64/Encoded types and re.Pattern. That is beyond the ask and earns no credit, but the guards are conservative (warn and fall back rather than raise), so the added risk is low and does not obscure the core fix. On correctness and tests B is clearly better; A is a valid but symptomatic, None-only workaround.

issue_md:
### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed the bug exists on the latest version of pydantic (2.13.4) and on current `main`.

### Python Version

3.13.14

### Pydantic Version

pydantic 2.13.4 / pydantic-core (latest from pip at time of report)

### Description

A model field annotated `SecretStr` with an **unvalidated `None` default** crashes serialization to JSON. Per [models docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/models/), field defaults are only validated when `validate_default=True`, so constructing such a model without arguments is legal — and every other scalar annotation serializes the unvalidated default as `null`. For `SecretStr`, however, `model_dump_json()` raises instead.

Note this is specific to the JSON path and to the *non-nullable* annotation:
* `model_dump()` (python mode) returns `None` fine;
* `Optional[SecretStr] = None` dumps to JSON correctly (`{"s":null}`);
* a control field `n: int = None` also dumps fine — so only the combination "non-nullable SecretStr + None default + JSON serializer" hits the broken path.

### Example Code

```python
import warnings
from typing import Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel, SecretStr

class M(BaseModel):
    n: int = None          # same pattern, control group
    s: SecretStr = None    # crashes

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as w:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    print(M().model_dump())          # {'n': None, 's': None}  -- OK
    try:
        print(M().model_dump_json())
    except Exception as e:
        print(type(e).__name__, "|", e)
    print("warnings emitted:", len(w))

class O(BaseModel):
    s: Optional[SecretStr] = None

print(O().model_dump_json())         # {"s":null} -- OK
```

### Actual behavior

```
{'n': None, 's': None}
PydanticSerializationError | Error calling function '_serialize_secret_field': AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get_secret_value'
warnings emitted: 0
{"s":null}
```

The exception escapes even though the value mismatch is exactly the situation the serialization layer normally degrades gracefully on (serialize as-is / warn). No `UserWarning` about the mismatched default is emitted either.

Looking at `_serialize_secret_field`, it calls `.get_secret_value()` unconditionally when the serializer runs with `when_used='always'`; there is no guard for `value is None` on a non-optional annotation, while core handles `None` defaults for other types before user serializers are reached.

### Expected behavior

Either of the consistent-with-everything-else outcomes:

1. serialize the unvalidated default as `null`: `{"n":null,"s":null}` (matching how `int = None`, `str = None` etc. behave), or
2. at minimum emit the standard serialization-mismatch `UserWarning` instead of raising an internal `AttributeError` wrapped into `PydanticSerializationError`.

The current traceback points users at pydantic internals rather than their own model definition.

title: Pipeline API `multiple_of()` rejects every `timedelta` and raises `TypeError` for `date`/`time`/`datetime`

judge.reasoning:
Patch B fixes the root cause in `_apply_constraint`: it introduces `_MULTIPLE_OF_SCHEMA_TYPES` covering the temporal types and applies `multiple_of` natively for them, mirroring the existing `_ORDERING_SCHEMA_TYPES`/`_LENGTH_SCHEMA_TYPES` pattern, while leaving `fraction` on the predicate path. It adds tests that check the core schema contents for date/time/datetime/timedelta, a Fraction predicate case, and a parity test against `Field(multiple_of=...)`. Independent tests confirm every reported scenario goes from failing on base to passing with B, with no regressions.

Patch A does not touch the pipeline API at all. It edits `_known_annotated_metadata.py` to remove `multiple_of` from the allowed constraints for date/time/datetime/timedelta, and also deletes `TIMEDELTA_CONSTRAINTS` and `TIME_CONSTRAINTS` (likely breaking other references). The reported pipeline bugs remain: timedelta exact multiples are still rejected and date/time/datetime still raise raw TypeError. Worse, it introduces a regression in the non-experimental API: `Field(multiple_of=2)` on date/time/datetime now raises `TypeError: Unable to apply constraint 'multiple_of'`, where the issue explicitly states this accepts today. It adds no tests. Patch A is the opposite of the issue's ask and breaks working behaviour.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

In the pipeline API, `multiple_of()` is broken for every temporal type. `timedelta` rejects **every** value, including exact multiples, and `date`/`time`/`datetime` raise a bare `TypeError` that escapes as-is instead of a `ValidationError`.

| annotation | `.multiple_of(...)` | `Field(multiple_of=...)` | correct |
|---|---|---|---|
| `int` | `multiple_of` error | `multiple_of` error | ✅ |
| `float` | `multiple_of` error | `multiple_of` error | ✅ |
| `Decimal` | `multiple_of` error | `multiple_of` error | ✅ |
| `Fraction` | predicate check | n/a (unsupported by core) | ✅ |
| `timedelta` | **rejects everything** | accepts | ❌ |
| `date` | **uncaught `TypeError`** | accepts | ❌ |
| `time` | **uncaught `TypeError`** | accepts | ❌ |
| `datetime` | **uncaught `TypeError`** | accepts | ❌ |

`validate_as(timedelta).multiple_of(timedelta(seconds=5))` rejects `timedelta(seconds=10)`, which is an exact multiple.

### Root cause

`_apply_constraint()` applies `multiple_of` natively only for a hardcoded `{'int', 'float', 'decimal'}`, and otherwise falls back to a Python predicate:

```python
def check_multiple_of(v: Any) -> bool:
    return v % multiple_of == 0
```

That predicate cannot work for temporal types:

* `timedelta(seconds=10) % timedelta(seconds=5)` is `timedelta(0)`, and `timedelta(0) == 0` is `False` in Python. The check therefore never holds, for any input.
* `date`, `time` and `datetime` do not support `%` at all, so the predicate raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for %`, which is not wrapped into a `ValidationError`.

This looks like an oversight rather than a decision. #13659 generalised exactly this pattern for the other constraints, introducing `_ORDERING_SCHEMA_TYPES` for `gt`/`ge`/`lt`/`le` and `_LENGTH_SCHEMA_TYPES` for `min_length`/`max_length`, both of which cover the temporal types. `MultipleOf` was left on its old hardcoded set in the same function.

Pydantic's own metadata already records the correct answer — `DATE_TIME_CONSTRAINTS` in `_known_annotated_metadata.py` includes `NUMERIC_CONSTRAINTS`, i.e. `multiple_of`:

```python
>>> from pydantic._internal._known_annotated_metadata import CONSTRAINTS_TO_ALLOWED_SCHEMAS
>>> sorted(CONSTRAINTS_TO_ALLOWED_SCHEMAS['multiple_of'])
['date', 'datetime', 'decimal', 'float', 'int', 'time', 'timedelta']
```

`fraction` is correctly absent there, and must keep using the predicate path — `fraction_schema()` takes no `multiple_of` argument, and `Fraction` supports `%` correctly.

### Suggested fix

Apply the constraint natively for the schema types that accept it, mirroring #13659:

```python
# Core schema types with native support for the `multiple_of` constraint:
_MULTIPLE_OF_SCHEMA_TYPES = frozenset({'int', 'float', 'decimal', 'date', 'time', 'datetime', 'timedelta'})
```

This aligns the pipeline API with the non-experimental API, per the position in #13564 that the two should agree. Note that this makes `multiple_of` a silent no-op on temporal types, because `pydantic-core` accepts the key but does not enforce it there — which is exactly what `Field(multiple_of=...)` already does today. Enforcing it would be a `pydantic-core` change and a separate discussion; this issue is only about the pipeline API diverging from `Field()`.

I have a fix and regression tests ready (the tests fail without the fix and pass with it, and `pyright` stays at its existing baseline). Happy to open a PR if I could be assigned.

### Example Code

```Python
import datetime
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import TypeAdapter
from pydantic.experimental.pipeline import validate_as

td = datetime.timedelta

# 1. timedelta: an exact multiple is rejected.
ta = TypeAdapter(Annotated[td, validate_as(td).multiple_of(td(seconds=5))])
ta.validate_python(td(seconds=10))
# ValidationError: Value error, Expected % 0:00:05 == 0
# (timedelta(0) == 0 is False, so the predicate never holds)

# 2. date/time/datetime: raw TypeError, not a ValidationError.
ta = TypeAdapter(Annotated[datetime.date, validate_as(datetime.date).multiple_of(2)])
ta.validate_python(datetime.date(2020, 1, 1))
# TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for %: 'datetime.date' and 'int'
```

```

title: `validate_call` cannot call a function with a keyword parameter named `self`

judge.reasoning: Both patches make the identical core change: `ValidateCallWrapper.__call__(self, /, *args, **kwargs)`, which is exactly the fix the issue proposes and resolves the root cause (the wrapper's bound `self` name colliding with a keyword argument). The independent tests confirm both pass all five scenarios, so correctness is equal on the reported issue. The difference is in tests and craft. Patch A adds a single minimal test with a positional-or-keyword `self` called by keyword; it would fail on base and pass after, but it does not cover the issue's literal example (keyword-only `self`), does not check that validation actually runs on the `self` argument, and does not cover `**kwargs` or async paths. Patch B's test exercises keyword-only `self` (the issue's exact case), positional-or-keyword passed both ways, `**kwargs` receiving `self`, the ValidationError `loc == ('self',)` showing validation now reaches the argument, and the async wrapper path. Patch B also applies the same positional-only fix to the deprecated `ValidatedFunction.init_model_instance`/`call` in `pydantic/deprecated/decorator.py`, which has the identical collision, and adds a matching test. That is adjacent work and earns no credit on its own, but it is the same root cause, is a one-token change per method, and adds no risk, so it does not count against B. With equal correctness and scope risk, B's substantially stronger test coverage decides it.

### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

`ValidateCallWrapper.__call__` is declared as `def __call__(self, *args, **kwargs)`, so the instance is bound to the name `self`. A decorated function with a keyword parameter literally named `self` can then never be called with it: `f(self=1)` raises `TypeError: ValidateCallWrapper.__call__() got multiple values for argument 'self'` before validation runs. The wrapped function itself is fine with that name; it is only the wrapper's signature that collides. Same in 2.12.5, 2.13.5 and `pydantic/_internal/_validate_call.py` on main.

Making `self` positional-only in `__call__` (`def __call__(self, /, *args, **kwargs)`) removes the collision without changing anything else. Can send the PR.

    return self


try:

title: Concurrent TypeAdapter construction raises RuntimeError on free-threaded Python

judge.reasoning: Both patches make the same core fix: iterate over `vars(typ).copy()` in `_decorator_infos_for_class` and snapshot `mappingproxy` namespaces in `LazyLocalNamespace.data`. Both pass all independent tests. The differences are in tests and scope. Patch A's tests are deterministic and run on every build: the `NamespaceMutator` `__class__` property trick mutates the TypedDict namespace during the `isinstance` check inside the decorator loop, so the test reliably fails on base and passes after, without depending on a free-threaded interpreter or timing. Its `LazyLocalNamespace` test likewise forces a mutation mid-merge via a hashing key, and the `dict.update()` implementation avoids per-item hashing so the test exercises the fix precisely. Patch A also hardens a third `vars(...).items()` site in `collect_known_metadata` with the same minimal change. Patch B's new tests are entirely skipped unless `sys._is_gil_enabled()` is False, so in a standard CI run they provide no regression coverage, and when they do run they are probabilistic. Patch B further rewrites `BaseModel.model_rebuild` to set mocks instead of deleting the schema/validator/serializer attributes. That is a behavioral change in a hot, user-facing code path unrelated to the reported TypedDict/TypeAdapter race; it may be a worthwhile thread-safety improvement, but it widens the blast radius of the fix and is only covered by tests that are skipped on GIL builds. A resolves the issue at the root, with deterministic tests and tighter scope.

### Description

Constructing separate `TypeAdapter` instances concurrently for the same new `TypedDict` can raise `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration` on free-threaded Python.

A full run produced 91 failures in 800 attempts with the GIL disabled and none with `PYTHON_GIL=1`. It also reproduces on Pydantic main at `1c8a330acc3077e77da64e3672c7c875fb4c6eaa`.

from __future__ import annotations

        value: int

        TypeAdapter(Record).validate_python({'value': '42'})

        list(executor.map(build, range(8)))

title: Three error-reference examples no longer raise the error they document, and the docs test suite cannot detect it

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the three stale examples identically in substance: a non-numeric input for `complex_type` (both inputs are confirmed in the issue to raise it and pass the independent tests), a `Callable` annotation for `invalid-for-json-schema`, and removal of the `string_sub_type` section. The independent tests pass on both, so correctness on the three reported examples is a wash.

The differences lie in tests and scope. Patch B adds `test_error_docs_examples_raise`, an AST-instrumented check that every `try`/`except` on the error pages actually enters its `except` branch. This is precisely the blind spot the issue describes and the test the reporter offered to write; it would have failed on base for all three examples and will catch the next #12498-style regression. B also keeps `test_validation_error_codes` consistent with a single explicit exclusion, mirroring the existing `timezone_offset` convention right above it. Patch A adds no test for the blind spot at all, so the docs can go silently stale again.

Patch A instead expands scope into pydantic-core, deleting the `StringSubType` variant from the Rust enum, the `ErrorType` Literal, and the core test table. The issue explicitly left that to the maintainers' judgement; removing a public error code from `ErrorType` is a user-facing API change (anyone matching on `'string_sub_type'` or using the Literal in typing now breaks) and belongs in a separate, deliberately reviewed change, not bundled with a docs fix. A also includes an unrelated edit to `docs/concepts/experimental.md` that has nothing to do with the issue. Neither of these earns credit, and the core removal adds real risk.

B resolves the issue, adds the regression test the issue asked for, and stays in scope. A fixes the same three examples but without a guard and with risky unrelated churn.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Three examples on the error-reference pages no longer raise the error they document, and the documentation test suite cannot detect it.

Every example on those pages has the same shape: do something that should fail, catch it, then print or assert the error code. The only assertion lives inside the `except` branch. When the operation stops failing, that branch never runs, so nothing is printed and no `assert` is evaluated. `run_print_check` compares printed output against the `#>` comments, and an example whose `print` never ran produces no output to disagree with, so the example exits 0 and CI stays green while the page documents behaviour that no longer exists.

I checked this exhaustively rather than by sampling. I injected a sentinel as the first statement of every `except` block on both error pages and ran each example. Of the 152 examples containing a `try`/`except` at v2.13.5, all 152 run, and exactly 3 never enter their `except` branch. On `main` the count is 3 of 157. None of the three is marked `test="skip"`, so all three are executed by CI today.

**1. `complex_type`, `docs/errors/validation_errors.md`**

`Model(num=False)` now validates successfully to `0j`, so the `#> 'complex_type'` line never prints. This changed in 2.13.0b1 with #12498, which made `complex` validation call the `complex()` constructor unconditionally in Python mode, and `complex(False)` is `0j`.

**2. `string_sub_type`, `docs/errors/validation_errors.md`**

The section says a strict `str` field rejects an instance of a `str` subclass. It does not: the example returns a plain `str` with the value `'foo'`, and `#> 'string_sub_type'` never prints. `pydantic_core` 2.49.0 still declares the error ("Input should be a string, not an instance of a subclass of str"), but I could not find any `str` schema that raises it. Building `core_schema.str_schema()` directly with `strict=True`, without strict, and with `strict=True` plus a pattern all accept a `str` subclass and return a plain `str`.

This looks intentional rather than accidental. #6261 reported exactly this behaviour as a bug in June 2023, was labelled `bug V2`, and was closed with the conversation moved to pydantic-core#786. So the check appears to have been removed on purpose and this documentation section was left behind describing it.

**3. `invalid-for-json-schema`, `docs/errors/usage_errors.md`**

`ImportString` has had a JSON schema since 2.8.0 via #9344, so `Model.model_json_schema()` succeeds and returns a plain string schema. The `assert exc_info.code == 'invalid-for-json-schema'` inside the `except` block has not executed since that release.

### Output of the example code below

Identical on 2.13.5 and on `main` at 2.14.0b2:

```
1. no exception; num = 0j
2. no exception; accepted 'foo'
3. no exception; {'properties': {'a': {'title': 'A', 'type': 'string'}}, 'required': ['a'], 'title': 'ImportStringModel', 'type': 'object'}
```

### Suggested fixes

1. `complex_type` is a one-word fix. `Model(num='not a complex number')` still raises `complex_type`, and so do `[]`, `{}` and a bare `object()`. Replacing `False` with any of those restores the example.
2. `string_sub_type` needs a decision rather than a fix, which is the main reason I am opening an issue instead of sending a patch. Given the trail through #6261, the section probably wants deleting rather than repairing, and possibly the error variant too, but that is your call.
3. `invalid-for-json-schema` needs a type that genuinely has no JSON schema, in place of `ImportString`.

Separately, the blind spot itself is fixable. If an example on these pages had to demonstrate that the error occurred, for instance by printing inside the `except` and also failing loudly when nothing was raised, then a future change like #12498 would turn the docs red instead of silently making a section untrue. I am happy to send a PR for any or all of this, including that check as a test, if you tell me which direction you prefer.

I used AI assistance to run this audit, in line with your AI policy. I have reproduced and understood each of the three cases myself and can explain any of them.

title: JSON schema ignores propagated config for stdlib dataclasses (`extra='forbid'` validates but no `additionalProperties: false`)

judge.reasoning: Both patches make the same core change: when a stdlib dataclass has no config of its own, `dataclass_schema` reads the propagated `extra_fields_behavior` from the dataclass's core-schema `config` (the same value validation uses) and feeds it to `_update_class_schema`. For every scenario in the issue (nested dataclass under a forbid model, `TypeAdapter(list[DC], config=...)`, allow/forbid/ignore) they behave identically, and the independent tests confirm both go from FAIL-ASSERT to PASS across all nine failing cases, including recursive, deeply nested, and shared-definition scenarios. Patch A's variant (merge `extra` into an existing config only if absent) is functionally equivalent to Patch B's `config is None` branch, since a dataclass with its own config never receives a propagated `extra_fields_behavior`. Neither is a symptom mask; both fix the root cause at the right place. The difference is in tests and clarity. Patch B adds three tests covering the model case parametrized over forbid/allow/ignore, the TypeAdapter and `TypeAdapter.json_schemas` paths, and a dedicated test for a dataclass reused in two fields plus a self-recursive dataclass, which directly exercises the definition-reuse concern its code comment explains (the dataclass schema may be a definition generated outside the current config-stack context). Patch A's parametrized test is also solid (covers DC with non-extra config, DC with its own extra, and pydantic dataclass) and it usefully repairs an existing test that was asserting `extra='ignore'` under a name claiming forbid. But A's test lacks the reuse/recursion/json_schemas coverage that matters most for the 'definition generated elsewhere' path. Patch B's explanatory comment is also clearer about why the core config is consulted rather than the current config wrapper. Scope and craft are otherwise comparable (A's long walrus line is slightly denser). On balance B edges out A on test coverage of the issue's implied scenarios.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

The docs ([Configuration propagation](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/config/#configuration-propagation)) say that configuration **is propagated** to stdlib dataclasses that don't set their own. Validation does this. JSON schema generation doesn't.

#10928 fixed this in the core-schema generator (`_internal/_generate_schema.py`) by changing the default so the parent's config is used:

```python
-            config = getattr(dataclass, '__pydantic_config__', ConfigDict())
+            config = getattr(dataclass, '__pydantic_config__', None)
```

The JSON-schema generator still has the same pattern. `GenerateJsonSchema.dataclass_schema` in `json_schema.py`, unchanged on `main`:

```python
config = cast('ConfigDict', getattr(cls, '__pydantic_config__', {}))

with self._config_wrapper_stack.push(config):
    json_schema = self.generate_inner(schema['schema']).copy()

self._update_class_schema(json_schema, cls, config)
```

`_update_class_schema` then decides `additionalProperties` from that `config`, which for a stdlib dataclass without its own config is always `{}`, whatever the parent says.

So with a parent `extra='forbid'`:

- the nested stdlib dataclass **rejects** unknown keys (`unexpected_keyword_argument`);
- its JSON schema doesn't say `additionalProperties: false`. Under JSON Schema rules, that means extra keys are allowed.

The schema and the validator disagree. This matters most where the schema is handed to a client that fills it in, such as LLM tool calling. The model is told extra keys are fine, then its answer is refused.

The same applies to `TypeAdapter(list[SomeStdlibDataclass], config=ConfigDict(extra='forbid'))`.

Expected: for a stdlib dataclass with no `__pydantic_config__`, `dataclass_schema` uses the propagated config (the one validation uses) when deciding `additionalProperties`, so `extra='forbid'` produces `additionalProperties: false`.

### Example Code

```python
import dataclasses

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, TypeAdapter, ValidationError


@dataclasses.dataclass
class Line:
    qty: int


class Order(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra='forbid')
    line: Line


try:
    Order.model_validate({'line': {'qty': 1, 'typo': 2}})
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e.errors()[0]['type'], e.errors()[0]['loc'])
    #> unexpected_keyword_argument ('line', 'typo')    <- propagated: forbid

schema = Order.model_json_schema()
print(schema.get('additionalProperties'))
#> False
print(schema['$defs']['Line'].get('additionalProperties'))
#> None    <- expected False

adapter = TypeAdapter(list[Line], config=ConfigDict(extra='forbid'))
try:
    adapter.validate_python([{'qty': 1, 'typo': 2}])
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e.errors()[0]['type'])
    #> unexpected_keyword_argument
print(adapter.json_schema()['$defs']['Line'].get('additionalProperties'))
#> None    <- expected False
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```text
             pydantic version: 2.13.5
        pydantic-core version: 2.46.5
          pydantic-core build: profile=release pgo=false
               python version: 3.14.7 (main, Aug 10 2026, 00:00:00) [GCC 16.1.1 20260515 (Red Hat 16.1.1-2)]
                     platform: Linux-7.1.3-200.fc44.x86_64-x86_64-with-glibc2.43
```

The snippet above reproduces on 2.12.5 and 2.13.5. 2.10.x and 2.11.x don't install on Python 3.14 here, but `dataclass_schema` has the same `getattr(cls, '__pydantic_config__', {})` default at `v2.10.1` and `v2.11.0`, and on `main`. So the split (validator inherits, JSON schema doesn't) looks present in every release since #10928 shipped in 2.10.1.

Related: #10917 / #10928 (the same fix, applied to the core schema only), #10785 (default `extra` for dataclasses/TypedDicts in JSON schema), #8326 (config can't be passed to `TypeAdapter` for a stdlib dataclass directly).

title: _FieldNameStack/_ModelTypeStack lose their pop() on exception, corrupting later unrelated schema builds

judge.reasoning: The production fix in `_generate_schema.py` is byte-for-byte identical in both patches: wrapping both `push()` yields in try/finally, which resolves the root cause. The difference is in tests and scope. Patch A adds two behaviour-level regression tests that reproduce the issue through real schema-generation paths: a nested `handler.generate_schema` failure caught in `__get_pydantic_core_schema__`, then asserting `handler.field_name` is None and that a `Self` field resolves to the enclosing model rather than the stale TypedDict. Both fail on base and pass after the fix, and they match exactly the user-visible corruption the independent tests also probed. Patch B's test in test_internal.py is also valid (it drives `GenerateSchema` directly and checks both stacks plus a later unrelated push, mirroring the issue's reproduction), but it asserts on internal attributes rather than observable behaviour. Patch B additionally changes `generic_recursion_self_type` in `_generics.py` and adds a test for it; that is a reasonable adjacent hardening but outside the issue's ask, earning no credit and mildly widening the review surface. With correctness equal, A's tighter scope and tests that verify the issue's consequences through public APIs give it a narrow edge.

issue_md:
## Description

`_FieldNameStack.push()` and `_ModelTypeStack.push()` in `pydantic/_internal/_generate_schema.py` (around lines 2910/2929) push onto their internal list, `yield`, then pop:

```python
@contextmanager
def push(self, field_name: str) -> Iterator[None]:
    self._stack.append(field_name)
    yield
    self._stack.pop()
```

If the code inside the `with self.field_name_stack.push(...):` block raises (schema generation is deeply recursive and can legitimately raise, e.g. `PydanticUserError` for a circular reference a few lines above this class in the same file), the `yield`'s continuation - the `.pop()` - never runs. The stale entry stays on the stack forever, and corrupts every *later*, otherwise-unrelated `push()`/`get()` on that same `GenerateSchema` instance, not just the one that failed.

## Reproduction

Isolated (no pydantic-core needed to demonstrate - this is pure Python control flow, verified against the actual class body copied verbatim):

```python
from contextlib import contextmanager

class _FieldNameStack:
    __slots__ = ('_stack',)
    def __init__(self):
        self._stack = []
    @contextmanager
    def push(self, field_name):
        self._stack.append(field_name)
        yield
        self._stack.pop()
    def get(self):
        return self._stack[-1] if self._stack else None

stack = _FieldNameStack()

try:
    with stack.push('some_field'):
        raise ValueError('boom')  # simulates any exception during schema generation
except ValueError:
    pass

print(stack.get())  # 'some_field' - already wrong, nothing is being processed

# The real damage: this leaks into a completely unrelated, later, successful push.
with stack.push('other_field'):
    pass
print(stack.get())  # 'some_field' again - should be None, 'other_field' was popped
                     # correctly but the stale entry underneath it was never cleared
```

Output:
```
some_field
some_field
```

Both lines should print `None`.

## Fix

Wrap the `yield` in `try`/`finally` so the pop runs unconditionally, the same guarantee a class-based context manager's `__exit__` gets for free:

```python
@contextmanager
def push(self, field_name: str) -> Iterator[None]:
    self._stack.append(field_name)
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        self._stack.pop()
```

Same fix applies identically to `_ModelTypeStack.push()` a few lines below - same shape, same bug.

I have a fix + regression test ready (asserts `.get()` returns `None` after a push whose body raised) and I'm happy to open a PR, per the note in the PR template about discussing non-trivial changes here first.

title: `FieldInfo.get_default` is 5-6x slower on 2.13 because of a relative import in the function body

judge.reasoning: The source changes in both patches are byte-identical: both hoist `smart_deepcopy` into the existing module-level `from ._utils import ...` line and delete the per-call relative import from `resolve_default_value`. This addresses the root cause named in the issue (the `resolve_name` cost paid on every call of the relative in-body import), and the independent tests confirm both patches move all six base failures to PASS. So correctness and scope are a wash. The difference is tests: Patch A adds none, so nothing would catch a regression if someone reintroduced a lazy import on this hot path. Patch B adds regression tests that record calls to `builtins.__import__` during `get_default()`, `model_construct()`, and private-attribute default resolution, asserting none occur. These would fail on the base commit (the independent harness used the same technique and saw `_utils` imports recorded on base) and pass after the fix, so they are non-tautological and cover the exact scenarios the issue describes, including the `model_construct` case and both `default`/`default_factory` branches. The tests warm up before recording and restore `__import__` via `monkeypatch.undo()`, which is careful enough. Monkeypatching `__import__` is slightly unusual but is the only direct way to assert the absence of an import statement, and it is scoped to the call under test. Patch B is the better fix because it delivers the same correct change plus meaningful protection against recurrence.

issue_md:
`FieldInfo.get_default()` costs about five to six times more on 2.13 than on 2.12.

On 2.13 the call is delegated to `pydantic._internal._fields.resolve_default_value`, whose body starts with a relative import that runs on every call:

```python
def resolve_default_value(...):
    from ._utils import smart_deepcopy
```

On 2.12 the plain-default branch was `return _utils.smart_deepcopy(self.default)`, with no import at call time. In 2.13 the import sits before the `default_factory` branch, so every call pays it.

`_fields.py` already has a module-level import from `._utils`, so the in-body import is not breaking an import cycle, and moving the name up adds nothing to import time.

Measured with `timeit`, best of 5 runs of 200000 calls:

| | 2.12.3 | 2.13.5 | 2.13.5, import moved up |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `FieldInfo(default=123)` | 55 ns | 300 ns | 85 ns |
| `FieldInfo(default_factory=list)` | 35 ns | 271 ns | 60 ns |

The cost is the import statement rather than module loading, since the module is already in `sys.modules`. With the relative form, `resolve_name` runs before the `sys.modules` lookup, so it is paid on every call even though the module is cached. A three-function package, identical except for the import form used to obtain the same callee:

| form | per call |
| --- | --- |
| `from ._helper import work` inside the body | 234 ns |
| `from pkg._helper import work` inside the body | 108 ns |
| module-level import | 32 ns |

Moving the import up removes most of the gap but not all of it. What is left is the extra `resolve_default_value` call and the sentinel checks added to `smart_deepcopy`.

This is visible in `model_construct()`, where `get_default` runs once per field. For a five-field model with defaults: 1.18 us on 2.12.3 against 2.49 us on 2.13.5. Passing every field explicitly, so that no default is resolved, gives 1.12 us on both.

### Version info

pydantic 2.13.5, CPython 3.13, macOS on arm64. The in-body import is still on `main`. Not measured on Linux or x86_64, so the absolute numbers will differ there, though the ratios should hold.

title: multiple_of=0 still raises ZeroDivisionError for non-native numeric types

judge.reasoning:
The issue identifies the root cause as the Python fallback in `_validators.py` doing `x % multiple_of` without validating the divisor, and names Fraction, temporal types, and complex as affected. Patch A fixes exactly that: it adds `check_multiple_of_constraint` and invokes it wherever the fallback `multiple_of_validator` is wired up (`apply_known_metadata`) and in the experimental pipeline's non-native branch. This covers Fraction, timedelta, complex, and also int/float/Decimal when they reach the fallback via a function schema (e.g. `AfterValidator`), which A tests explicitly. It also rejects negative, NaN and infinite divisors, matching pydantic-core's message for native types. The check is tolerant of non-numeric constraint values (TypeError falls through to the existing validation-time error), and the only existing-test edit (changing `multiple_of: 0` to `1` on list/set/frozenset cases) is a necessary adjustment so those tests still exercise the 'cannot apply constraint' path rather than the new schema check. Tests are broad and would fail before the change.

Patch B instead adds native `multiple_of` support to the Rust Fraction and TimeDelta validators and routes those two types to core. That resolves the reproduction and passes the independent tests, but it does not touch the Python fallback at all, so `complex` and any int/float/Decimal constraint that lands on a function schema still raise `ZeroDivisionError` at validation time. It is also a larger, riskier change (new Rust validation logic, core schema TypedDict changes, i128 microsecond arithmetic, a new feature surface) that depends on a coordinated pydantic-core change, and its validity checks only reject <= 0, not NaN/inf for Fraction (less relevant) while leaving the generic path unguarded. B's new feature work earns no credit on its own and here it obscures that the reported root cause remains.

A is more correct against the issue as stated, better tested across the affected types, and tighter in scope.

issue_md:
### Description

`Field(multiple_of=0)` is rejected during schema generation for `int`, `float`, and `Decimal`, but equivalent non-native numeric types still pass schema generation and raise an uncaught `ZeroDivisionError` during validation.

### Reproduction

```python
from fractions import Fraction
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class Model(BaseModel):
    value: Fraction = Field(multiple_of=0)

Model(value=Fraction(1, 2))
```

Actual: validation raises `ZeroDivisionError` rather than `ValidationError`.

Expected: model definition fails with a schema-generation error stating that `multiple_of` must be greater than zero, consistently with native numeric types.

The Python fallback in `pydantic/_internal/_validators.py` performs `x % multiple_of` without validating the divisor. `Fraction`, temporal types, and `complex` use this fallback. I found no existing report for the remaining types after the native numeric fix.

title: `ZoneInfo` validation raises `IsADirectoryError`/`OSError` instead of `ValidationError` for some invalid keys

judge.reasoning: The production change is byte-for-byte identical in both patches: adding `OSError` to the caught exceptions in `validate_str_is_valid_iana_tz`, which is the root-cause fix the issue asks for. Both pass all independent tests. The difference is in tests and scope. Patch A deletes `tests/test_types_zoneinfo.py` and recreates it as `tests/types/test_zoneinfo.py`, rewriting every existing test from `BaseModel` to `TypeAdapter` form. That file move and rewrite is unrelated churn that obscures the actual fix in the diff and changes the `loc` and assertions of pre-existing tests for no reason tied to the issue. Its only regression test is environment-dependent: on Python 3.13 `'America'` raises `ZoneInfoNotFoundError` and would pass even without the fix, and whether `'a'*300` hits `ENAMETOOLONG` depends on platform and tzdata presence. Patch B appends to the existing test file, adds the same environment-dependent cases (plus `Etc`), and crucially adds a monkeypatched test that forces `IsADirectoryError` and a plain `OSError` out of `ZoneInfo`, guaranteeing the new except branch is exercised on every CI configuration. The monkeypatch targets the module-global `ZoneInfo` name that the validator looks up at call time, so it works. B also adds a short comment explaining why `OSError` is caught, which helps future readers. B is better on tests, scope, and craft.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Validating a `ZoneInfo` field with certain invalid strings raises a raw `OSError` subclass instead of a `ValidationError`:

- A tz database *directory* name such as `'America'`, `'Europe'` or `'Etc'` raises `IsADirectoryError` on Python 3.10–3.12 when the `tzdata` package is installed (`tzdata` is a pydantic dependency on Windows and is also pulled in by e.g. pandas). CPython only started converting this case to `ZoneInfoNotFoundError` in 3.13 (gh-85702).
- An over-long key (e.g. 300 characters) raises `OSError: [Errno 63] File name too long` (reproduced on Python 3.12 with `tzdata`, and on Python 3.13 on macOS without it).

`validate_str_is_valid_iana_tz` in `pydantic/_internal/_validators.py` only catches `(ZoneInfoNotFoundError, ValueError, TypeError)`, so these errors propagate unchanged. Expected: a `zoneinfo_str` validation error, the same as for `'Not/AZone'`. For example, in a web API that validates a user-supplied timezone, these inputs currently produce an unhandled exception instead of a validation error.

Suggested fix: add `OSError` to the caught exceptions. I have a small patch with a regression test ready if this is welcome.

### Example Code

```python
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Model(BaseModel):
    tz: ZoneInfo

Model(tz='Not/AZone')  # ValidationError (expected)
Model(tz='America')    # IsADirectoryError: [Errno 21] Is a directory: '.../site-packages/tzdata/zoneinfo/America'
Model(tz='a' * 300)    # OSError: [Errno 63] File name too long: '...'
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```
             pydantic version: 2.14.0b2
        pydantic-core version: 2.49.0
          pydantic-core build: profile=release pgo=false
               python version: 3.12.13 (main, Jun 11 2026, 03:55:21) [Clang 22.1.3 ]
                     platform: macOS-15.3.1-arm64-arm-64bit
             related packages: email-validator-2.3.0 typing_extensions-4.16.0
                       commit: e2ac21dcd
```
(tzdata is installed in this environment)

Disclosure: found, reproduced and the draft fix tested locally with the help of an AI coding agent (Claude Code); reviewed before filing.
